items.title: Mitigating the Negative Consequences of Work Stressors: The Role of Perceived Meaning and Calling
items.abstract: The purpose of the present study was to understand how meaningful work and vocational calling may benefit employees’ work and well-being under circumstances of job stressors. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources framework, we tested a model linking stressor exposure to work and health outcomes through one’s experience of meaningful work, and dependent on one’s perception of work calling via a two time-point survey of 493 employees. Exposure to particular stressors and evaluated workplace and health-relevant outcomes were consistently linked, and further support was found for the role of calling in buffering the impact of certain stressors on outcomes through work meaning. This study contributes to the occupational health and career development literatures by expanding our understanding of detriments to job-related (i.e., job satisfaction and turnover intentions) and well-being-related (i.e., physical symptoms and burnout) criterion variables from workplace stressors. Implications for organizations and counselors, study limitations, and future directions are discussed.

items.title: MobHeteroCAS: Mobility-Aware DNN Task Scheduling in Heterogeneous Collaborative Autonomous Systems
items.abstract: Scene perception for situational awareness is crucial for autonomous agents like UGVs and UAVs that involves sensing from different 2D and 3D modalities to execute tasks such as semantic segmentation and object detection. However, UGVs and UAVs face limitations in power and computation capacity. To address these challenges, we propose an offloading framework called MobHeteroCAS , designed to leverage nearby peer autonomous vehicles for computation. Our framework addresses key challenges in offloading DNN (Deep Neural Networks) tasks in a collaborative environment: (a) Optimally offloading data/features to leverage nearby devices’ computation capabilities; (b) Reducing offloaded data for efficient communication in low-bandwidth environments; (c) MobHeteroCAS determines the optimal ”split ratio” to determine how much data should be offloaded to each nearby device based on network parameters such as RSSI values, latency incurred due to network conditions, workload, memory constraints (CPU, GPU, RAM), and power limitations. The key contribution of MobHeteroCAS is determining the optimal split ratio in stationary and mobile environments. Apart from the devices consuming more power and memory when they are mobile, the latency increases when the distance between communicating devices increases. Thus, MobHeteroCAS estimate the latency to offload the computation when devices are on mobile before selecting the optimal split ratio. MobHeteroCAS is truly fault-tolerant, incorporating the identification of device (agent) failure and task redistribution when a device fails. We empirically demonstrate that offloading DNN features instead of raw images reduces overall system latency. Therefore, we offload feature representations of raw images for tasks such as image classification and semantic segmentation. In our study, we utilize a testbed comprising three Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) and one Linux laptop, implementing a self-adaptive optimization framework capable of managing multiple heterogeneous tasks collaboratively across multiple nodes. Our evaluations, involving simultaneous execution of multiple DNN tasks like Image Classification and Semantic Segmentation, demonstrate that employing a split ratio of 30%-42%-28% (data distribution across auxiliary nodes) reduces offloading latency by approximately 72% (from 38 \(ms/data\) to 10.5 \(ms/data\) ) compared to compressed frames and reduces total operation time by approximately 99% (from 281.33 minutes to 169 seconds) compared to the baseline configuration (execution on the primary node) in stationary setting. The latency improves by 78-82%.

items.title: More Than a Score: Reinforcement Learning with Verbalized Feedback for Generative Recommendation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for generative recommendation, where recommended items are generated directly from users' interaction histories. To further improve recommendation quality, reinforcement learning (RL) has been applied to align these models with recommendation objectives. However, existing RL methods rely on scalar rewards to implicitly guide exploration. These rewards do not specify which aspects of a candidate conflict with the user's preferences or how the next candidate should differ. To address this gap, we propose VerRec, a verbalized feedback-guided RL framework for generative recommendation. Specifically, a user simulator generates personalized verbalized feedback based on the user's historical preferences and the candidate item profile. The policy uses this feedback to produce refined recommendations. Original and refined candidates form an expanded group and are jointly optimized with group relative policy optimization. The user simulator is only required during training and is removed at inference time. Experiments on three Amazon review datasets with two generative recommendation backbones demonstrate that VerRec improves recommendation accuracy and ranking quality. Further analyses show that verbalized guidance encourages exploration of more diverse candidates and helps the policy discover more rewarding recommendations during training.

items.title: More than a Second Pair of Eyes: Artificial Intelligence Across the Breast Imaging Pathway
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from stand-alone accuracy studies to prospective deployment across breast screening, risk prediction, multimodal diagnosis, treatment response, and workflow support. The goal of this narrative review is to determine which AI applications have demonstrated clinical benefit, which remain technically promising, and what safeguards are required for implementation. We synthesize randomized trials, prospective cohorts, real-world implementations, external validations, systematic reviews, and guidance identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus through 30 June 2026. In screening, AI-supported mammography can increase cancer detection and reduce reading workload, but effects depend on whether AI is used as concurrent support, an independent reader, triage, or partial autonomy; autonomous workflows may shift work and cost downstream through additional recalls. MASAI met its prespecified noninferiority criterion for interval cancer, but this should not be interpreted as proof of equivalence or mortality benefit. Image-based risk models often discriminate better than density or conventional clinical models, although prospective benefit from AI-guided allocation to supplemental imaging has not yet been demonstrated. Evidence for contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM), MRI, ultrasound, radiomics, and multimodal models is less mature and limited by external validation, domain shift, missing data, operator dependence, and uncertain incremental value beyond clinicopathological factors. Ungrounded large language models and opaque foundation models are not suitable for autonomous clinical advice. Current evidence therefore supports controlled, task-specific integration rather than radiologist replacement; real clinical benefit depends on governance of the whole AI-enabled pathway, including local validation, human factors, downstream resource use, statistical stopping rules, and fallback procedures.

items.title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents
items.abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.

items.title: Multi-View Synergistic Learning with Vision-Language Adaptation for Low-Resource Biomedical Image Classification
items.abstract: Accurate biomedical image classification under limited supervision remains challenging due to scarce annotations, subtle inter-class differences, and complex disease semantics. Pretrained vision-language models offer a promising foundation for alleviating data scarcity through knowledge transfer, yet effectively adapting them to low-resource biomedical tasks remains nontrivial. To this end, we propose Multi-View Synergistic Learning (MVSL), a unified framework that jointly considers three complementary perspectives: adaptation paradigms, representation granularity, and disease semantic relationships. Specifically, MVSL adopts tailored adaptation strategies for visual and textual encoders, accommodating their distinct representational characteristics while preserving pretrained knowledge. To capture both holistic image semantics and localized pathological evidence, we introduce multi-granularity contrastive learning that aligns global image representations and local visual features with disease-specific textual embeddings. Furthermore, we develop a Disease Semantic Graph (DSG) that leverages disease descriptions generated by large language models to model class-level semantic relationships and regularize adapted textual representations, thereby complementing discriminative learning and helping mitigate excessive specialization toward observed categories. Through the synergy of these complementary perspectives, MVSL enhances fine-grained discrimination while supporting semantic consistency and generalization to unseen categories. Extensive experiments on 11 public biomedical datasets spanning 9 imaging modalities and 10 anatomical regions demonstrate the effectiveness of MVSL in few-shot classification and base-to-novel generalization. The implementation and detailed experimental results are publicly available at https://github.com/luoxiaoliu/MVSL.

items.title: Multidimensional ageing reserve and 10-year all-cause mortality among older adults in China: a prospective cohort study of the Chinese longitudinal healthy longevity survey
items.abstract: Background Dietary, behavioral, psychological, and engagement resources may jointly be associated with survival in later life. We examined the association between a multidimensional ageing reserve (MDAR) index and all-cause mortality among older Chinese adults. Methods The 2008–2009 baseline data from the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS) were linked to subsequent mortality records. MDAR combined four equally weighted standardized domains: dietary diversity, lifestyle behavior, psychosocial wellbeing, and activity/social-cognitive engagement. Follow-up was censored at 10 years. Cox models compared MDAR quartiles and estimated a linear summary association per standard deviation (SD). Restricted cubic splines assessed non-linearity. Complete-case analyses were supplemented by multiple imputation, a 2-year landmark analysis, attained-age models, and weighted analyses. Results Among the 10,249 participants (mean age 85.2 years; 53.7% women), 6,569 deaths occurred over 51,534 person-years. Fully adjusted hazard ratios (HRs; 95% confidence intervals [CIs]) relative to the lowest quartile were 0.94 (0.88–1.01), 0.99 (0.92–1.06), and 0.85 (0.78–0.93) for quartiles 2, 3, and 4, respectively. The linear summary hazard ratio per SD was 0.93 (0.90–0.96). The spline indicated non-linearity ( p = 0.007), with a more pronounced inverse association at higher scores. Activity and social-cognitive engagement had the clearest association in mutually adjusted domain models (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.89–0.95). The pooled estimate after covariate multiple imputation was 0.93 (0.90–0.96); the 2-year landmark estimate was 0.95 (0.91–0.99). Conclusion Higher MDAR was associated with lower mortality, particularly at higher score levels. The association weakened after adjusting for health, function, and cognition. Selection, residual confounding, and overlap between the index and functional capacity limit causal interpretation; the results do not establish that increasing MDAR would prolong life.

items.title: Multimodal Physiological and EEG Responses to Short‐Term Hypobaric Hypoxia Exposure: Evidence of Central–Peripheral Coordination
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Low‐pressure environments are common in aircraft cabins and high‐altitude operations, where reduced oxygen partial pressure alters human physiological regulation, energy metabolism, and cognitive performance. However, existing studies primarily focus on isolated physiological responses, lacking a systematic understanding of the coupling between central neural activity and peripheral physiological adaptation under short‐term hypobaric hypoxia exposure. In this study, a controlled experiment was conducted in a hypobaric chamber under three pressure conditions (101.3, 67.2, and 56.1 kPa). Multimodal data, including electroencephalography (EEG), heart rate (HR), blood oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ), and respiratory‐metabolic parameters, were synchronously collected to characterize human responses across pressure levels and exposure time. Results showed that decreasing pressure significantly increased metabolic demand, with HR rising by 3.7%–5.8%, SpO 2 decreasing from 98.2% to 86.5%, and respiratory rate and metabolic rate markedly elevated, indicating typical hypoxic compensation. At the neural level, EEG spectral power shifted from low‐frequency (δ and θ) to high‐frequency (α and β) bands, with enhanced activity in frontal and occipital regions, suggesting increased cognitive resource allocation. Significant correlations between EEG features and peripheral physiological indices further revealed a coordinated central–peripheral coupling mechanism. This study provides a novel integrative perspective linking environmental pressure, metabolic cost, and neural regulation, offering new insights for cabin pressure design, human performance assessment, and human–environment interaction modeling in built environments.

items.title: Navigating curricular complexity: Programmatic assessment and AI in a business context
items.abstract: Traditional models of programmatic assessment are historically rooted in highly structured, linear disciplines such as medicine (Heeneman et al., 2015; Torre et al., 2021). Translating these principles to a diverse, modular Business and Economics faculty presents profound curricular, structural, and governance challenges. Business courses within Monash University operate within a flexible architecture designed to support highly personalized student pathways, where over 90% of students have unique pathways via diverse combinations of majors, minors, and electives. Consequently, units are highly interconnected—sometimes contributing to up to 20 distinct programs—so that an assessment alteration in one unit ripples across multiple independent degree structures. This structural friction is compounded by distributed governance split across separate academic departments, departmental Directors of Education (DOEs), Course Directors, and Chief Examiners. To navigate this complex landscape, the Senior Educational Designer and the Associate Dean of Learning and Teaching (ADLT) collaborated on a university-wide initiative entitled Programmatic Assessment and Artificial Intelligence Review (PAAIR) spurred by TEQSA requirements (Lodge et al., 2023). We adapted established theory around programmatic assessment to synthesize a tailored five-principle framework, designating “Collaborative and Transparent Culture” as Principle 1. To address modular friction, we drew on Dawson’s (2020) concept of programmatic assessment security, shifting the unit of analysis from hardening every individual, isolated module to strategically securing key programmatic assessment moments across the entire course. Cultivating this shared-accountability mindset was critical because curriculum reviews occurred by course, where a single unit could feed into multiple programs with diverse departmental oversight. It was difficult to have a unified, static “full picture” of a complete course at any one stage of a review, as some units may have been completed as part of other reviews, or they may be dual-coded with a postgraduate course, requiring complex cross-referencing across courses, departments, year levels, and campuses. To bridge this diagnostic gap, we collaborated with the faculty’s data analytics team to develop the PAAIR Dashboard in PowerBI. Serving as an interactive visual analytics platform, the dashboard empowers DOEs, Course Leaders, and Educational Designers to see beyond disciplinary silos, map competency coverage across shared pathways, monitor assessment distributions, and facilitate data-informed co-design conversations in real time. It helps flag structural gaps—such as when a core graduate competency is not assessed under secure conditions at least twice per year level—ensuring curriculum resilience across highly complex student pathways. At the launch of the project, we developed a comprehensive suite of guidelines to support Unit Learning Outcome (ULO) refinement, Course Learning Outcome (CLO) mapping, and balanced assessment design. These guidelines have been instrumental in improving our course designs by scaffolding competencies progressively and designing assessment tasks with and without generative AI (Lodge et al., 2023; Matheis & John, 2024). This dual approach balances the educative, values-driven framework of academic integrity with the adversarial, hardening requirements of assessment security (Dawson, 2020). As the initiative now enters the initial transition to Business-As-Usual (BAU) operations, we are actively developing a future governance strategy to manage subsequent curriculum changes sustainably. This Pecha Kucha presentation delivers a transparent roadmap and strategic recommendations for other modular higher education faculties seeking to operationalize programmatic assessment and AI review within highly complex, non-linear educational ecosystems.

items.title: Negotiating identity and relationality: An AI-enhanced polylogue on human-centred learning design practices
items.abstract: This poster presents a developing AI-enhanced polylogue methodology and conceptual framing to understand how third-space professionals in higher education are negotiating their shifting roles and identities while designing human-centred learning and assessment. Recent technological disruptions (e.g., widespread proliferation, advancement and use of generative AI, focus on cybersecurity, adoption of data-enabled technologies and ecosystems) have intensified tensions around higher education assessment structures and practices, exposing the limitations of isolated, task-based evaluation of student learning (Boud et al., 2020; Corbin et al., 2025). In response to the challenges posed to learning and assessment in the contemporary higher education landscape, emerging scholarship has foregrounded relationality and human connection alongside a shift to more program-wide approaches to assessment and assurance of learning (Lodge et al., 2023; Nicola-Richmond et al., 2025). This has highlighted questions about how educators can sustain meaningful relationships with each other and with students amidst these disruptions (Maldon et al., 2025). In this work-in-progress project, we focus on these relational questions and explore how technological disruptions are reshaping the roles and identities of educators, specifically curriculum designers working in third-space roles at the boundary of academic and professional domains (Whitchurch, 2012). We build on work that positions teaching and learning as fundamentally relational, emphasising connection, trust, care, and dialogue between educators, students, and third-space professionals (Riddle & Hickey, 2023). Our aim is to understand how relationality may be conceptualised in the context of transforming curriculum to support human flourishing and critical engagement with generative AI in our everyday learning design practice, particularly in the design of program-level assessment, feedback, mentorship, and collaborative sense-making structures. The project employs an AI-enhanced polylogue methodology inspired by Markauskaite et al. (2022). The AI-enhanced polylogue is a structured, multi-voiced inquiry, where participants engage in iterative cycles of individual reflection and collaborative dialogue, involving AI as a reflective interlocutor to surface gaps, alternative perspectives, and assumptions. Over several months, three curriculum designers independently responded to targeted questions in reflective logbooks, then engaged in semi-structured conversations about connection in higher education, program-level learning design, evolving educator roles, and the contributions of third-space professionals. This was complemented by a collaborative chat with a generative AI tool, in which participants used AI to probe gaps, tensions, and alternative perspectives arising from the conversations. These strands are then brought together in collaborative critical reflection sessions to identify emerging patterns in relational practice and their significance in program-level curriculum design. This poster shares early themes from the logbooks and conversations. Early analysis highlights how participants experience and navigate tensions between increasing technological mediation alongside their third-space roles and their commitment to relational practice. The importance of human-centred learning design and its implications will also be examined and shared. The project contributes to contemporary discussions on inter-collegial practices that keep connection, trust, and dialogue central in increasingly AI-mediated educational environments. As part of this project, participants treat disruption as an invitation to remake educator identities and practices in more relational, collaborative, and inclusive ways.

items.title: Network-Exposed Configuration Attacks on LLM-Controlled Social Robots
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in embodied robots create security dependencies beyond inference. We investigate a network-exposed configuration attack on the Pollen Robotics Reachy Mini Lite, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to replace personality settings and the cloud LLM's system prompt through a management interface, without adversarial conversational input. Eleven prompt-injection attempts across five categories were reported as resisted, whereas both configuration-layer attack paths produced observable behavioural changes on physical hardware. We demonstrate local and network-adjacent access, mapping the weakness to CWE-306 (Missing Authentication for a Critical Function) and CWE-1327 (Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address), with a reported CVSS v3.1 score of 6.5 (Medium). A configuration endpoint also accepts cross-origin requests without a CORS preflight (CWE-352; 6.5 Medium), while the persistent-memory sink stores content without enforcing its stated restrictions. A source review of 59 public repositories identifies missing authentication in 10 of 11 source-verifiable genuine applications, or 11 of 11 including a framework-default case. These findings indicate recurrence within the sampled repositories, not prevalence in commercial products. We characterise a deployment gap between developer-oriented network assumptions and consumer-facing embodied AI security: inference-layer refusal cannot prevent unauthorised changes to model instructions. Potential consequences include surveillance through onboard cameras and microphones and social engineering of nearby users. Proof-of-concept code, evidence and the survey are available at https://bit.ly/reachypi.

items.title: Neural tracking of phonological, lexical, and syntactic surprisal during naturalistic listening in elementary-aged children with and without dyslexia
items.abstract: Children with dyslexia show persistent phonological difficulties in controlled experiments yet often comprehend everyday spoken language successfully. The present study examined how children with and without dyslexia neurally track phonological, lexical, and syntactic information during naturalistic story listening, and how this tracking relates to reading proficiency. Children listened to a story during functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Study 1 examined neural tracking in 140 typically developing (TD) children. Study 2 compared children with dyslexia with age- and gender-matched TD controls (n = 35 per group). Large language model-derived surprisal estimates indexed tracking at each level at exploratory and multiple comparison corrected thresholds. In TD children, each level of surprisal tracking showed a distinct cortical profile, and higher reading comprehension was associated with greater phonological and syntactic tracking, but reduced lexical tracking. Children with dyslexia also showed distinct tracking profiles across levels. In this group, however, higher reading proficiency was associated with greater lexical and syntactic tracking and reduced phonological tracking. Group contrasts mirrored these patterns. Children with and without dyslexia differ in how neural tracking of linguistic information relates to reading. In dyslexia, reduced phonological tracking alongside greater lexical tracking may reflect increased reliance on higher-level linguistic information. Syntactic tracking was positively related to reading proficiency in both groups, consistent with the protracted development of syntax and its contribution to literacy. These findings offer new insights into the real-time neurobiology of naturalistic language comprehension and how the interaction of underlying skills may vary in children with dyslexia.

items.title: Next-generation high performance MXene–MgF2 based wideband solar absorber with artificial intelligent optimization for renewable energy mining applications
items.abstract: Solar energy provides a promising and easily accessible renewable energy source when it comes to solving energy issues. Industries consume high amounts of energy for various uses. Thus, the concept of a solar absorber that absorbs wideband radiation is shown in this study. The absorber's configuration is MXene-Magnesium Fluoride-MXene. These structures create a novel geometry that traps the heat and absorbs a high amount of radiation. The proposed absorber's resonator layer geometry has a T-shape with a Nanodisk MXene-based resonator Solar Absorber, whose structure makes it polarization-insensitive. An average of 95.57% absorption was achieved within the range of 200-3000 nm, keeping absorptance above 96% over a bandwidth nm while exceeding 92% over a much wider bandwidth of around 2120 nm across the spectral spectrum under investigation. Moreover, this suggested absorber achieved 94.9% average absorption under AM 1.5. Examined several solar absorber structures and the findings. Optimized the design over several parameters and examined the outcome. Then, analyzed the Transverse Electric and magnetic fields with magnetic and electric colour-changing fields, which are described in the results section. The research presents clear engineering outcomes for solar thermal absorber design, with machine learning methods demonstrating the application of artificial intelligence in the study. The examination shows that the Machine Learning model's maximum achievable R 2 value of 0.93 for parameter change intends to minimize the simulation period by a quarter when compared with older methods, while minimizing other simulation needs. The high absorption rate with a unique resonator design is promising for applications as a renewable solar dryer for mining.

items.title: Nobody writes for the reader: Reading level in paediatric health guidance, real health queries and AI chatbot responses
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose To compare the reading level of paediatric health guidance, parents' own questions and artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot responses to those questions, and to test whether chatbots adapt to the reading level of the person asking. Methods Cross-sectional study, reported following the Chatbot Assessment Reporting Tool (CHART), of 18,392 guideline pages (17,516 family-facing, 876 clinician-facing) from 86 organisations, 1,000 parent-authored questions sampled from 23,477 public forum posts, and 5,000 responses to those questions from five commercially deployed chatbots. Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL) was the primary outcome, with six secondary metrics. In a sub-study, 100 questions were resubmitted with an instruction to match the reader's level or to answer at sixth-grade level (1,500 responses). Results Median FKGL was 12.51 for clinician-facing guidance, 9.08 for family-facing guidance, 8.37 for chatbot responses and 6.15 for parents' questions. The American Medical Association sixth-grade standard was exceeded by 99.3% of clinician-facing pages, 92.6% of family-facing pages and 89.2% of chatbot responses. Every chatbot answered above the reading level of the question asked (median difference + 1.21 to + 3.57 grades). Given an explicit sixth-grade instruction, the median gap narrowed in every model and three of five answered below the reader's level. Conclusion Paediatric health information from institutions and chatbots alike is written above the level of its readers. Chatbots do not adapt to the reader by default, but can when instructed.

items.title: Nonlinear function regression using quantum ensemble learning
items.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and quantum technologies have driven the emergence of quantum machine learning, yet imperfections in near-term quantum devices remain a major obstacle for achieving practical quantum advantage. In the absence of fault-tolerant machines, ensemble learning, which combines multiple imperfect quantum devices, may unlock new quantum computing applications. Here, we introduce two ensemble-learning algorithms, namely Bagging and AdaBoost, for enhancing the accuracy of nonlinear regression problems. While Bagging trains variational quantum regressors independently, AdaBoost employs a sequential training strategy and achieves significantly better prediction accuracy. By incorporating systematic feature selection into our ensemble learning algorithms, we enhance their predictive power for highly nonlinear functions. We further improve prediction accuracy through a feature-to-qubit mapping strategy based on repeated feature encoding. The performance of our ensemble-based algorithms improves with both the number of regressors in the ensemble and the size of each regressor. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using four benchmarking functions with varying degrees of nonlinearity by relying on a feature pool limited to first- and second-order polynomial terms.

items.title: NVIDIA Kumo Tabular: Pushing the Accuracy$\unicode{8211}$Efficiency Frontier for Tabular Prediction
items.abstract: We introduce Kumo Tabular, a family of open tabular foundation models for classification and regression, in three sizes: Kumo Tabular-S (27M parameters), Kumo Tabular-M (61M), and Kumo Tabular-L (214M). Pretrained only on artificial tables from the Kumo prior, they can make predictions on new tables without any training. In our approach, a table encoder compresses each row into an embedding, and an in-context learning transformer predicts the unlabeled rows from the labeled ones. Kumo Tabular introduces architectural innovations that improve both training stability and predictive performance, enabling the model to scale up to 150M cells on modern GPUs. Kumo Tabular-L ranks first on eight benchmarks: TabArena, TALENT, BeyondArena, ScoringBench, STRABLE, MulTaBench, RamanBench, and TabBench-Bio. These cover probabilistic regression, tables with over 1M rows or 100K columns, and tables with strings, text, or images. Accuracy improves with model size in all tested comparisons. All three sizes lie on the accuracy-speed frontiers of TabArena and BeyondArena. Kumo Tabular-L predicts faster than the runners-up, LimiX-2 on TabArena (36 times) and TabPFN-3.5 on BeyondArena (1.7 times). Weights and pretraining code are released under OpenMDW-1.1 and Apache 2.0, respectively.

items.title: OAK-Mind: Zero-Training Mental Health Change Inference from Passive Sensing via Knowledge-Grounded Multi-Agent LLMs
items.abstract: Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{OAK-Mind}, a zer\textbf{O}-training, multi-\textbf{A}gent, \textbf{K}nowledge-grounded LLM pipeline for inferring mental health changes from passive sensing data. The pipeline organizes sensing data into behavioral dimensions including sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, and orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes. It synthesizes their assessments and applies questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline assessment with human-readable rationale grounded in observed behavioral patterns and domain knowledge. Across datasets and prediction tasks, while without task-specific training, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples. It also demonstrate consistent improvement upon direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones. Ablation analyses support the benefits of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, distributing analysis across domain-specific agents, and incorporating domain knowledge. Our findings highlight the potential of knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs for training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.

items.title: Occupational health-oriented reinforcement learning models for intelligent adjustment of college students’ employment stress
items.abstract: Abstract The stress of work is a significant issue in the occupational health arena for college students because of the uncertainty of employment, evolving labor market expectations and preparation for the world of work. The existing methods are mainly based on psychological assessment instead of intelligent adjustment of stress according to the occupational health. This study is to design an Adaptive Vortex Optimizer (AVO) based Attention-Based Dueling Deep Q-Network (AD-DQN) model for intelligent adjustment of college students'' employment stress based on personalized decision optimization. The Occupational Employment Stress dataset consists of 15,000 student responses from multiple data sources, including university career guidance, health questionnaires, academic profiles, internship experiences, and students'' self-reported stress responses. Imputation using the K-Nearest Neighbor, Min–Max normalization and outlier refinement are used to enhance data quality. Deep Autoencoder-based feature extraction aims to obtain compact representation by capturing salient occupational, behavioral and educational traits and removing redundant information. The proposed model is designed to use extracted features to optimize the learning parameters and exploration strategies using AVO for efficient convergence. An Attention Mechanism (AM) selects important occupational health and employment related stress signals whereas a Dueling DQN is used to construct an intervention policy for an individual by estimating state value and action advantage. Feedback is offered and the RL constantly adjusts recommendations, thereby furthering career readiness and stress regulation. Experiments conducted in Python show superior performance in terms of 0.982 Accuracy, 0.963 Recall, 0.97 AUC, 0.94 F1-Score and 0.91 Kappa when compared to existing models. From these results, the classification reliability and discriminative ability have been improved, balanced prediction performance and consistent decision making have been achieved. AVO-AD-DQN can support university career-counseling services by enabling personalized employment-stress assessment and adaptive stress-management recommendations.

items.title: OmniTongue: A Comprehensive MLLM Benchmark for Automated Tongue Diagnosis in Traditional Chinese Medicine
items.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have excelled in Western medical imaging, yet their potential in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) tongue diagnosis remains systematically unevaluated. Tongue diagnosis requires sophisticated global and local perception, serving as a rigorous touchstone for assessing the visual understanding depth of MLLMs. However, existing datasets are limited by single dimensions, coarse granularity, and ambiguous labels, hindering the evaluation of authentic clinical capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce OmniTongue, the first comprehensive, fine-grained Visual Question Answering benchmark for TCM tongue diagnosis. This benchmark integrates 1,351 expert-validated images and 21,616 instruction pairs. Its core design features 16 clinical dimensions for multidimensional evaluation, region-specific annotations for pathological localization, and 66 fine-grained labels for precise diagnostic representation. items.title: Orchestrate: An AI-secure MarTech simulation for systems thinking and industry-ready capability
items.abstract: Marketing technology (MarTech) education has traditionally emphasised the acquisition of discrete platform skills, often resulting in fragmented, “tool-first” approaches that inadequately prepare graduates to manage complex MarTech ecosystems. At the same time, the rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has intensified concerns about whether conventional assessment designs can validly evaluate higher-order capabilities such as judgement, strategic reasoning, and decision making (Corbin et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2024). These converging challenges highlight an urgent need for Technology Enhanced Learning (TEL) innovations grounded in human-centred design that foster systems thinking and strategic decision making while providing authentic, AI-resilient assessment opportunities. This presentation introduces Orchestrate, a low-fidelity (LoFi) MarTech simulation designed to cultivate systems thinking and assess industry-ready capability development in undergraduate and postgraduate marketing programs. Developed in Microsoft Excel, a widely available and low-barrier technology, the simulation provides a scalable and accessible learning experience. Informed by industry practice, Orchestrate positions students as marketing leaders responsible for managing investments across an interconnected MarTech ecosystem. Piloted during Semester 1, 2026, with Bachelor of Commerce students undertaking the Marketing Technology major at RMIT University, student teams balanced competing priorities to optimise customer acquisition, retention, satisfaction, and revenue growth. Rather than learning isolated technologies, students allocated finite budgets across 12 capability areas aligned to the People, Process, Data, and Technology (PPDT) framework (Monshizada et al., 2023). The pedagogical design is underpinned by systems thinking theory, which emphasises understanding interdependencies, trade-offs, and emergent patterns within complex systems (York et al., 2019). The simulation makes relationships between MarTech capabilities explicit, demonstrating that sustainable organisational performance emerges from balancing people, process, data, and technological priorities rather than investing in individual tools. Authentic assessment principles further situate learning within realistic professional contexts that mirror contemporary marketing practice. A distinctive contribution of Orchestrate lies in its AI-resilient assessment design. Rather than relying on static written outputs that can readily be generated or enhanced by GenAI, assessment focuses on students’ situated decision making within the dynamic simulation environment. Teams must justify their evolving strategies, explain the consequences of their choices, and demonstrate alignment between investment decisions, course principles, and organisational performance outcomes. Because gameplay produces different conditions and outcomes for each team, the design reduces opportunities for inappropriate AI assistance while maintaining a focus on higher-order judgement and strategic reasoning. Early evidence from the Semester 1, 2026 pilot indicates strong student engagement and learning. Assessment submissions demonstrated sustained engagement with the simulation, while reflective responses showed strong understanding of course concepts and application of relevant theoretical frameworks to strategic decisions. Qualitative student experience survey feedback also identified Orchestrate as a key highlight of the course. These findings are indicative rather than the result of a formal research evaluation; a comprehensive Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) study is now being developed, with an ethics application underway, to investigate the simulation’s impact on systems thinking, strategic decision making, student engagement, and learning outcomes.

items.title: People before technology? What do learning designers across sectors see as essential for successful practice?
items.abstract: Positioned at the intersection of pedagogy, technology, and curriculum design, learning designers play an increasingly important role in the design, development, and enhancement of learning experiences across diverse educational contexts. Their work has been described as being characterised by collaboration, relationship-building, and the ability to facilitate change within complex educational environments (Altena et al. 2025; Walji, 2023). Recent research further suggests that effective learning design depends on adaptive relational work, trust, openness, and the integration of diverse forms of expertise across interdisciplinary teams (Papageorgiou & Bennett, 2026). Existing studies have explored learning designers’ demographic profiles, qualifications, professional backgrounds, career pathways, job titles, and professional positioning, particularly within higher education (Altena et al., 2025; Gilmore & Nguyen, 2023; Mitchell et al., 2017; Slade et al., 2019). Learning designers have also been conceptualised as “third-space” or hybrid professionals whose work spans pedagogical, technological, and organisational boundaries (Bennett, 2023; Whitchurch, 2012), and competency frameworks have been proposed to describe their professional capabilities (MacLean & Scott, 2011; Simpson, 2025). However, there remains limited evidence about learning designers working outside higher education and little empirical research examining how learning designers themselves perceive the knowledge, skills, and values that underpin successful professional practice. This presentation reports preliminary findings from a larger survey of 268 learning designers working in Australia (88%) and New Zealand (5%) across diverse contexts, including formal education (K–12 and tertiary), enterprise, government, and not-for-profit organisations. The presentation focuses on respondents’ perceptions of the knowledge, skills, and values that constitute the “special sauce” of learning design practice. Data was collected through a cross-sectional online survey and participation was on a voluntary basis. The findings suggest that learning designers perceive the human-centred dimensions of their work as more central to their professional practice than the technical dimensions commonly associated with the role. Collaboration with subject matter experts was the most frequently reported task performed by learning designers and interpersonal skills were the most frequently selected skill, highlighting the collaborative and relational nature of the role. A high proportion of respondents identified knowledge of learning and motivation theories as a core knowledge domain underpinning effective learning design practice, followed by knowledge of educational technologies and digital learning environments. Strong emphasis was also placed on proficiency with learning management systems as an essential skill. The values identified by respondents further suggest the profession’s strong orientation toward critical thinking, empathy, and adaptability. While technological knowledge and skills were widely recognised as important, particularly educational technology and digital learning environments, and learning management systems, they were identified slightly less frequently than the human-centred aspects of the role. These findings suggest that, although technology is an important component of learning design practice, practitioners primarily appear to prioritise collaboration, learner support, and the application of human judgement as essential to the role rather than technological expertise alone. The presentation concludes by arguing that, as artificial intelligence and automation increasingly undertake routine technical and production tasks, the future value of learning designers may lie less in the technologies they can use and more in their uniquely human capabilities, including empathy, communication, collaboration, critical judgement, and the ability to bring people together around better learning experiences. In this sense, the “special sauce” of learning design practice may not be technological expertise but people skills. Moving the field forward will therefore require a stronger sociological and philosophical foundation for understanding how these human capabilities can be developed, valued, and sustained as educational technologies continue to evolve.

items.title: PERSONAL AUTONOMY – A KEY COMPETENCE DEVELOPED DURING PHYSICAL EDUCATION CLASSES
items.abstract: Background. Personal autonomy represents one of the key competencies of modern education, playing a decisive role in the development of intrinsic motivation, responsibility, and students’ active involvement in the educational process. Physical education provides a privileged framework for the development of autonomy, as motor activities involve decision-making, cooperation, self-regulation, and the evaluation of personal progress. The purpose of the present study is to analyze the role of personal autonomy as a key competence developed during physical education classes and to highlight the impact of student-centered teaching strategies on motivation, perceived competence, and social integration. The research findings indicate that promoting autonomy significantly contributes to increased involvement, psychosocial well-being, and motor performance. The objectives of the research are: identifying the teaching strategies that promote autonomy; assessing the level of students’ involvement and motivation; analyzing the effects of autonomy on psychosocial well-being. The following methods were used in conducting the study: documentary analysis of specialized literature; systematic pedagogical observation; a questionnaire for assessing autonomy and motivation; comparative analysis of the obtained results. Results. The analysis of the obtained data highlights a significant increase in the level of intrinsic motivation and student involvement. The participants demonstrated greater responsibility for their own progress, an enhanced capacity for self-organization, and improved social relationships within group activities. Furthermore, a reduction in anxiety and an increase in self-esteem were observed as a result of active involvement in the processes of decision-making and self-assessment. Conclusion. In conclusion, personal autonomy represents a fundamental key competence in physical education, contributing to the motor, cognitive, social, and emotional development of students. The implementation of student-centered teaching strategies promotes intrinsic motivation, responsibility, and active involvement in the educational process.

items.title: Pixel is All You Need
items.abstract: Text, images, audio, touch, and even robot actions can, in principle, all be rendered onto a single canvas, suggesting an ambitious goal of unifying all modalities within vision. Language provides the natural first test. To subsume it, a visual model must reason directly over text in pixels. Across a wide range of image, video, and unified multimodal generators, however, we find that their visual generation modules cannot perform symbolic reasoning over text on the canvas. They succeed only when an underlying text module or prompt rewriter already supplies the answer, effectively reducing the generator to a mere renderer, a limitation that post-training does little to resolve. To test whether this failure stems from pixels themselves or from current training paradigms, we train a family of purely pixel-space generative models from scratch without any text pathway. With images as their sole input and output, these models read questions, write intermediate steps, and produce answers directly on the canvas. Remarkably, they exhibit hallmark behaviors of large language models. Performance improves predictably with scale following a power law. Writing intermediate steps frame by frame substantially outperforms single-frame answering, echoing chain-of-thought, while reinforcement-learning post-training further strengthens reasoning. Moreover, sharing one canvas allows the same model to reason across modalities, a capability that text-only language models lack. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of these phenomena in purely pixel-space generative models free of text tokens.

items.title: Practice-Dependent Development of Discernment: How Doing Can Change What Can Later Be Distinguished
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Practice-Dependent Development of Discernment, an account of how repeated practice with correction can develop a capacity to discriminate that receiving a statement once does not secure. Retained wording, correct performance on practiced cases, and transferable discernment are separate achievements. The account assesses discernment through demonstrated discrimination across specified new cases, with the conditions of practice and feedback recorded. Exposure to a rule, repetition, and success on familiar examples do not alone establish transfer. Statements can accelerate learning and sometimes do much of the work that practice would otherwise do, while repetition without correction can entrench error. The assessment asks what was stated, what was practiced, how errors were corrected, and whether performance transfers under the conditions in which the capacity will be used. The discussion sets the mechanism beside Ericsson, Krampe, and Tesch-Römer’s account of deliberate practice and examines two documented cases. Tanaka, Curran, and Sheinberg’s 2005 bird-identification study compared species-level and family-level training with equal exposure and corrective feedback. The species-level advantage transferred to new photographs of trained species; for entirely new species, it was significant for wading birds but not owls. Accounts of Nainoa Thompson’s training under Mau Piailug and the 1980 voyages of Hōkūle‘a trace the development of wayfinding through corrected practice at sea. Piailug made decisive interventions on the outbound passage. On the return, Thompson made most navigational decisions while his teacher remained aboard but largely kept out of the navigation. Part of the Relational Conditions and Dynamics series within On Human Modeling, the paper examines who arranges practice, supplies correction, defines adequate discernment, and tests transfer. Potential applications in human–AI research include tutoring, training design, and competence assessment that distinguish repeating a rule or succeeding on familiar tasks from discriminating correctly in new cases under specified conditions.

items.title: Prevalence, risk factors, and ergonomic intervention needs for musculoskeletal pain: a nationwide survey of Korean endoscopists
items.abstract: Background/Aims Despite the increasing endoscopic volume and complexity in Korea, comprehensive data on the musculoskeletal health of gastrointestinal endoscopists remains limited. This study examined the prevalence, risk factors, and interventions related to musculoskeletal pain in Korea. Methods A nationwide cross-sectional web survey was conducted in November 2023. We analyzed responses from 209 endoscopists regarding demographics, practice patterns, symptoms, and ergonomic behaviors using multivariate logistic regression to identify factors associated with musculoskeletal pain. Results Among the respondents, 72.2% reported musculoskeletal pain, most frequently in the hand/wrist/fingers (57.4%) and shoulders (51.7%). Objective workload showed an apparent threshold-like pattern associated with the overall pain (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 2.18 for high workload; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.09–4.36). In contrast, perceived procedural burden was a robust independent predictor for both overall pain (aOR, 2.29; 95% CI, 1.50–3.50) and site-specific pain, particularly the neck (aOR, 1.88) and hand/wrist/fingers (aOR, 1.71). While 42.1% used general ergonomic aids, 70.3% expressed willingness to adopt endoscopy-specific devices. Conclusions Musculoskeletal pain is prevalent among endoscopists in Korea. Objective workload was associated with overall pain susceptibility, showing a threshold-like pattern, whereas perceived procedural burden was independently associated with both overall and site-specific symptoms. These findings highlight the need for targeted ergonomic interventions and endoscopy-specific technologies.

items.title: PrimateX: a unified multi-agentic framework for standardized MRI analysis across primate species
items.abstract: Abstract Standardized preprocessing has transformed human neuroimaging into a reproducible, population-scale enterprise, yet equivalent computational frameworks for non-human primates (NHPs) remain absent, forcing continued reliance on fragmented, labor-intensive workflows. Here we introduce PrimateX, a multi-agentic computational framework in which LLM-guided orchestration dynamically routes structural MRI scans through species-tailored, topology-preserving workflows, extracting cortical surfaces directly from raw volumes with full provenance tracking across marmosets, macaques, chimpanzees, and humans. Validated on 1,221 NHP and 1,113 human scans, PrimateX outperformed existing NHP pipelines in segmentation and surface reconstruction while matching dedicated human tools such as FSL in their native domain. Through MRI-style data augmentation, the framework achieved robust zero-shot generalization to 8 unseen primate species across 31 cohorts from 19 global sites (n = 157). Critically, the routing architecture and closed-loop quality-control mechanisms, demonstrated through diverse downstream neuroimaging analyses and cross-species research, establish PrimateX as a widely-applicable computational paradigm. PrimateX is available at https://primatex.pku.edu.cn.

items.abstract: Relevance. The effectiveness of public administration in the sphere of security is determined not only by the resource capacity of individual security and defence sector actors, but primarily by the quality of their horizontal interaction under dynamic hybrid threats. The experience of repelling massed missile and drone strikes on Ukraine’s critical infrastructure in 2022–2024 has shown that departmental data fragmentation, functional duplication, and the absence of formalized interaction protocols among the intelligence community, civil protection forces, and critical infrastructure operators significantly reduce the speed and quality of administrative decisions. Aim. The article aims to diagnose the key problems of interagency coordination in the sphere of state security of Ukraine and to substantiate organizational mechanisms for solving them. Objectives: to identify typical determinants of interagency interaction inefficiency; to demonstrate, using the "detection – alerting – response" chain during massed strikes on energy infrastructure, how data fragmentation translates into a loss of response time; to develop the authors’ previously proposed resilience mechanisms into operational proposals; to assess the potential of existing digital situational-awareness platforms for expanding coordination beyond the military domain. Methods. Systemic and comparative analysis of foreign coordination models, case study, structural-logical modelling. Results. Five systemic determinants of coordination inefficiency were identified: hierarchy instead of networking; departmental data fragmentation; unformalized interaction protocols; legal gaps in the distribution of powers; and the absence of an institutionalized lessons-learned cycle. The case study demonstrated a gap between military intelligence information and civilian response. An organizational-legal mechanism for overcoming this gap is substantiated, based on extending the architecture of an existing situational-awareness platform to non-military coordination actors. Conclusions. Eliminating interagency fragmentation requires a shift from a hierarchical to a network-centric security governance model, the institutionalization of subsidiarity-based response protocols, and a legally embedded lessons-learned cycle.

items.title: Productivity Without Prosperity? Who Captures the Economic Gains from Workplace Artificial Intelligence?
items.abstract: Abstract Experiments show that generative AI raises productivity on specific tasks by 14 to 40 percent, but who benefits when it spreads through the economy is far less clear. This study builds a capture accounting from task to economy. It links published field and survey evidence on productivity gains, adoption and wage pass-through to an exact decomposition of productivity gains in the U.S. nonfarm business sector, using the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) release of 5 November 2026 and the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey. Between the first quarter of 2024 and the third quarter of 2026, output per hour rose by 6.35 log points; 3.28 points (51.7 percent; rounding interval 50.3 to 53.1) reached workers as higher compensation relative to output prices, and 3.07 points went to nonlabor income as the labor share fell to 53.0 percent, the lowest since 1947. Labor’s capture fell from 84 percent in 2024 to 70 percent in 2025 and turned negative (-16 percent) in the four quarters to 2026 Q3, while nonfinancial corporate unit profits rose 16.1 percent. At the worker level, Danish administrative data show only 3 to 7 percent of productivity gains reaching earnings. A consistency bound combining these pass-through rates with plausible shares of AI in productivity growth implies that AI explains a minority of the rise in nonlabor capture (median 23 percent; 5th to 95th percentile 8 to 38 percent) and cannot be the whole story. The evidence is descriptive and aggregate, and the AI shares are bounds, not estimates. Purpose - This study asks who captures the economic gains from workplace AI, and how much of the recent shift in the distribution of productivity gains could plausibly be attributed to it. Design/methodology/approach - The paper combines published task-level, worker-level and firm-level evidence with an exact capture decomposition of BLS quarterly data, rounding-error Monte Carlo intervals, and a consistency analysis that bounds the AI contribution using pass-through rates and adoption arithmetic. Findings - Roughly half of the recent productivity gain went to workers and half to nonlabor income, with workers’ share falling over time and turning negative in the latest quarters. AI use is concentrated in large firms and in information and finance. Pass-through of AI-specific gains to workers is small, but AI can account for only a minority of the shift. Research limitations/implications - Aggregate indexes are rounded and revised, AI shares of productivity growth are not observed, and field studies are not representative of the economy. The analysis cannot identify causal effects. Practical implications - Bargaining institutions, training and transparency over how time savings are used are likely to determine capture, and policy should track labor’s share of gains alongside productivity. Social implications - Productivity growth need not translate into prosperity for workers, and young entrants in exposed occupations face distinct employment risk. Originality/value - The paper provides a transparent accounting that connects micro and macro evidence on AI’s distributional effects and quantifies what current data can and cannot say.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

items.title: Prompting inclusion: Development of a GenAI prototype to support UDL-aligned course design in computing education
items.abstract: Universal Design for Learning (UDL) offers a valuable framework for developing inclusive and accessible courses, but educators often receive limited support in translating its broad principles into context-specific teaching and assessment practices. This paper reports on the design of a custom generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) conversational assistant prototype developed to support computing educators in Australian tertiary education in applying UDL to their courses. The prototype provides concrete, non-directive suggestions across the three tenets of UDL, multiple means of engagement, representation, action and expression. Rather than treating GenAI as a generic automation tool, the prototype explores how prompt design, scope limitation, structured outputs, and persona-informed contexts can scaffold inclusive pedagogical reflection while maintaining academic judgement. The paper presents the functional prototype as its primary contribution and describes its design considerations, prompt architecture, and early scenario-based testing.

items.title: Public opinion surveys with large language models: methodological opportunities and validity risks
items.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being considered as tools for computational social science, yet their implications for survey and public-opinion research remain insufficiently understood. This study examines whether and how they can serve as methodological instruments for estimating aggregate public opinion under out-of-sample conditions. Across three studies, commercial and open-source LLMs are evaluated against recent Pew Research Centre surveys. Study 1 shows that GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 can approximate national-level response distributions more accurately than uniform, normal-distribution, and historical-average baselines, with GPT-4 achieving mean absolute errors of approximately 4–8.5%. However, the models also exhibit important threats to validity, including underrepresentation of Republican viewpoints, underestimation of uncertainty, and, in some cases, overly homogeneous response distributions. Study 2 extends the analysis to GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, and Llama 3.3, showing that aggregate predictive accuracy generalises across models but that partisan alignment and distributional fidelity are model- and topic-dependent. Study 3 demonstrates that collective-level estimation is more valid than aggregating persona-based individual simulations, which produce substantially higher error and stronger homogeneity bias. Ablation tests further indicate that predictions are relatively robust to role prompts and temperature settings but sensitive to survey-item context. These findings suggest that LLMs may be useful as exploratory and supplementary tools in public-opinion research. However, the responsible use of LLMs requires explicit validation against human data, attention to bias and uncertainty, and careful integration with established principles of survey design.

items.title: PVTSizing 2.0: A Fast and Reliable Analog Circuit Sizing Operator for Agentic EDA Workflows
items.abstract: Analog circuit design automation requires both coordinated tool execution and efficient numerical search. Large language models (LLMs) offer new ways to organize tool execution, but finding one sizing that satisfies specifications across process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners remains costly. PVTSizing 2.0 addresses these needs through a human-agent workflow built around an independently usable numerical optimizer. An agent carries the designer's approved task through execution and result review. The optimizer reduces unnecessary training through loss-guided updates and uses critic-guided local refinement to explore additional candidates while accounting for cross-corner conflicts. An optional LLM adviser supplies parameter relationships to focus numerical search on circuit-informed directions, while the optimizer selects adjustment amplitudes and verifies their effects through simulation. Across four circuit benchmarks, the standalone optimizer completes all 40 runs and achieves a 7.3x speedup in overall mean runtime over the original PVTSizing, with a comparable mean sample count. In a separate study, the best tested knowledge-injection configuration further reduces mean runtime by 39.9% and simulation samples by 35.4% relative to the standalone optimizer.

items.title: Rebalancing the algorithm: A sociotechnical approach
items.abstract: While education shifts further into the digital age, human connection remains irreplaceable. Effective learning is fundamentally a deeply social process, where robust relationships with peers, educators, and communities are indispensable to cognitive, emotional, and ethical development (Noddings, 2013; Vygotsky, 1978). As higher education is increasingly shaped by advanced digital technologies including Generative AI and AI-enabled learning systems, it is essential that educational innovation moves beyond technological capability to consider how advanced technologies can foster human connection, cultivate belonging, support collaboration, and enhance individual and collective wellbeing (Holmes et al., 2019; UNESCO, 2023). This view aligns well with Fink’s (2013) taxonomy of significant learning, which recognises that understanding oneself and others (the human dimension) is a critical component of learning, an integrated process comprising six interrelated dimensions. Cultivating this dimension is vital for developing new values and interests that sustain life-wide and life-long learning, and advance learners’ academic and personal development. With life-wide and life-long learning in mind, we extend Chen’s (2025) learning taxonomy approach that is grounded in Bloom’s (1956) and Fink’s (2013) learning taxonomies to adopt a sociotechnical approach to the design of a postgraduate Information Systems (IS) unit. We designed learning activities and assessments that not only develop disciplinary knowledge and skills required to achieve unit learning outcomes but also empower students to cultivate new values and interests that sustain life-wide and life-long learning. Student feedback and reflection have been positive, suggesting that this approach fosters deep engagement, enhances meaningful learning and increases students’ metacognitive development. We will share key reflections from our teaching practice and invite discussion to explore how sociotechnical approaches can inform the design of AI-enabled IS education to advance life-wide and life-long learning.

items.title: Rebuilding and rehumanising the University of Trust in an era of generative distrust
items.abstract: As higher education institutions accelerate the adoption of generative AI, questions of trust, human agency, and educational purpose are becoming central to the future of technology mediated education. This paper argues that AI has not created a crisis in higher education so much as exposed and accelerated declining trust within teaching, learning, and assessment. Drawing on Humboldt’s conception of the university as a site of productive living tensions, this disciplined provocation examines how technology-mediated education is reshaping the relationships between learners, educators, knowledge, and algorithms. Drawing on inductive theory generated from a two-year constructivist grounded theory study, this paper proposes the notion of epistemic crisis as a way to represent the deficit dialogue driving epistemic change, and the concept of generative distrust exposing the fractures between the productive living tensions that build trust in higher education. The paper contributes to contemporary debates on human-centred learning design by arguing for a rebalancing of the algorithm through pedagogies that foreground care, collegiality, civic engagement, controlled risk and collective mission.

items.title: Recent Advances in Medical Imaging Segmentation: Generative, Few-Shot, Foundation and Universal Models
items.abstract: Medical imaging is a cornerstone of modern healthcare, driving advancements in diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient care. Among its various tasks, segmentation remains one of the most challenging problems due to factors such as data accessibility, annotation complexity, structural variability, variation in medical imaging modalities, and privacy constraints. Despite recent progress, achieving robust generalization and domain adaptation remains a significant hurdle, particularly given the resource-intensive nature of some proposed models and their reliance on domain expertise. This survey explores cutting-edge advancements in medical image segmentation, focusing on methodologies such as Generative AI, Few-Shot Learning, Foundation Models, and Universal Models. These approaches offer promising solutions to longstanding challenges. We provide a comprehensive overview of the theoretical foundations, state-of-the-art techniques, and recent applications of these methods. Finally, we discuss inherent limitations, unresolved issues, and future research directions aimed at enhancing the practicality and accessibility of segmentation models in medical imaging. We maintain a GitHub Repository to continue tracking and updating innovations in this field.

items.title: Recipient-Focused Hallucinations in AI-Generated Professor Outreach Emails: A Pilot Factorial Evaluation of Grounding and Verification
items.abstract: Abstract Background : LLMs increasingly draft personalized academic outreach, which depends on describing a real professor's research. Unsupported claims about a recipient's topics, methods, or findings misrepresent their scholarly work. Methods : In an offline pilot, a 2 × 2 design varied whether the writer received a publication evidence packet during drafting and whether a verifier revised the draft afterwards (conditions A–D). We generated 96 emails for 12 professors across three fields, decomposed them into 360 atomic research claims, and labelled each against the professor's evidence packet with an automatic (LLM) evaluator. All primary estimates are pilot estimates from automatic labels, not human-verified measurements. Reliability was assessed against a blinded 36-claim human-labeled subset (10% of claims) and a second automatic evaluator from a third model family. items.title: Reclaiming wonder: Creating meaningful learning experiences in a digital age
items.abstract: The past two decades have seen higher education progressively rely on digital-enabled teaching and learning systems. Learning management systems, lecture recordings, online readings, assessment technologies, and increasingly flexible modes of participation have transformed the student experience (The University of Queensland, 2021, 2025, 2026a, 2026b). In this context, digital technologies have become an essential and expected component of contemporary higher education (The University of Queensland, 2021, 2026a). This Pecha Kucha explores how the rapid evolution of educational technology, culminating with the emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), is prompting educators and students to reconsider questions of authenticity, trust, creativity, and what makes learning memorable, meaningful and distinctly human (Lao et al., 2026; Polyportis, 2023; Rajan & Niranjan, 2025). As GenAI becomes embedded in education, learners are increasingly navigating blurred boundaries between real and generated experiences (Çalli & Alma Çalli, 2025; Lao et al., 2026; Weikmann et al., 2025). Content that once inspired fascination, curiosity, or wonder is increasingly met with scepticism (Çalli & Alma Çalli, 2025; Weikmann et al., 2025). This raises questions about what forms of learning remain uniquely valuable when information, content creation and digital assistance are readily available (Polyportis, 2023; Rajan & Niranjan, 2025). The challenge facing higher education is not whether technology belongs in learning environments, but how it can be meaningfully used to engage students in the learning process. Two examples illustrate this approach. In a humanities literature course, students engaged with the University of Queensland library collections and spaces before developing creative responses to course texts through zines, journals or rewritten scenes. Students could work in paper-based or digital formats, supporting creativity, personal expression and engagement with disciplinary ideas. The resulting exhibition demonstrated diverse interpretations of course concepts and encouraged ownership of learning. In an archaeology course, Gradescope was used to support assessment and feedback processes while learning remained centred on collaborative, in-person activities, creating a tangible “mycelium web” of theory, mapping relationships between concepts into a shared physical artefact. This approach supported collaboration, deeper conceptual understanding and the practical application of theory through active participation. In both examples, technology played a supporting role, enabling greater focus on curiosity, creativity, connection and meaningful learning experiences. While digital technologies have created opportunities for access, flexibility, and inclusion that were previously impossible, educators also have a responsibility to design learning experiences that cultivate curiosity, creativity, human connection, and shared discovery (Rajan & Niranjan, 2025; The University of Queensland, 2021, 2025, 2026a). Yet educators face challenges in selecting appropriate technologies, meeting assessment security requirements, and guiding students in the ethical use of GenAI and the development of human values (Al-Shamaileh et al., 2026; Qin et al., 2025; The University of Queensland, 2026b). Learning designers and other third-space professionals contribute expertise in bringing educators, technologies and human-centred pedagogies together to create engaging learning activities and assessment. Through these examples, attendees will be encouraged to consider how learning environments can foster connection, trust, and engagement in an increasingly AI-mediated world. They will gain practical insights into using technology strategically while preserving the human qualities of learning that foster curiosity, belonging, and participation.

items.title: Reconfiguring Authenticity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Critical Code Analysis of Deepfake Generation and Detection Systems
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines how authenticity is constructed and reconfigured within deepfake generation and detection systems. Drawing on the perspective of Science and Technology Studies (STS) and the methodological framework of Critical Technical Practice (CTP), it conducts a critical analysis of the core code of two representative open-source projects, FaceFusion and DeepfakeBench. Through the syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic dimensions of code, the study investigates how authenticity judgments are technically operationalized within deepfake systems. The findings reveal three interrelated processes through which authenticity is reconfigured in deepfake technological systems. First, authenticity undergoes Proxyization, as direct judgment of authenticity itself is increasingly suspended and verisimilitude comes to function as its technological proxy. Second, authenticity undergoes Riskification, as authenticity judgment shifts from factual verification to risk calculation and risk balancing. Third, authenticity undergoes Residualization, as technological systems establish authenticity by continuously identifying and excluding falsity. Consequently, authenticity no longer functions as a positive category requiring direct confirmation. Instead, it becomes a negative category established through the negation of falsity and exists only as the residual state left after falsity has been continuously identified and excluded. More importantly, these processes demonstrate that deepfake technologies are driving a profound transformation of the digital information environment: credibility is increasingly established through the exclusion of falsity rather than the confirmation of truth, thereby reshaping the fundamental logic through which authenticity is established and trust is sustained within the broader social information environment.
