items.title: Reflections on women in academic leadership as a community for education-focused academics
items.abstract: Education-focused academics are important to learning and teaching in Australian higher education yet often face fragmented academic identities and uncertain promotion pathways within research-intensive cultures that reward research over educational expertise (Fleischner & Lutze-Mann, 2025). These challenges are often amplified for women across a range of academic and higher education career pathways, including roles spanning academic and professional domains. Education-focused expertise is frequently respected externally yet under-recognised within academics’ own institutions, compounding isolation and invisibility (Brown et al., 2024). This poster shares the collective reflections of education-focused women from Curtin University, The University of Queensland, The University of Sydney and The University of Western Australia, connected through the ASCILITE Women in Academic Leadership (WiAL) program. Established in 2021 to address women's underrepresentation in senior academic roles, WiAL operates as a cross-institutional community of practice built on structured mentoring, peer coaching, webinars and regular connection (Bone et al., 2024). Drawing on reflective narratives and examples, we explore how the WiAL community operated as collaborative professional learning, drawing strength from our diverse perspectives and perseverance through the inevitable tensions of education-focused work. With a shared interest in technology-enhanced learning, we make sense of our academic identities across markedly different institutional conditions for education-focused work. We outline how the community supported tangible career outcomes: preparing for and achieving promotion, pursuing learning and teaching grants, building publication momentum, and naming and disarming imposter syndrome. Connections forged through the network have already generated scholarly collaboration, including contributions to a cross-institutional edited collection on generative AI in learning and teaching (Fitzgerald, 2025; Vallis, 2025). Institutional evidence confirms that education-focused academics progress to the most senior levels when career development, connection and recognition are deliberately cultivated (Fleischner & Lutze-Mann, 2025). Mentoring structured across institutions and free of institutional hierarchies builds capability while countering the isolation experienced by women at the nexus of education and technology (Gribble et al., 2024). Our experiences affirm that such communities foster visibility, gravitas and relationships (Brown et al., 2024), enabling collective strength over individual competition. Sustained digitally across four states, our community models the conference theme: connection, collaboration and compassion enacted through technology. We share practical insights into reflective career communities that can build resilient and sustainable education-focused careers through meaningful, technology-mediated connection.

items.title: Reframing academic integrity in Australian universities for the Generative AI era
items.abstract: This paper reports initial findings on how the top 10 Australian universities have responded to Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) through their academic integrity policies, guidelines, and AI-related governance documents. Using qualitative policy analysis and thematic analysis of institutional policies and guidelines, this study examines how GenAI use is framed and governed, including how institutional expectations are communicated to students, academics, and administrators. The study also explores how universities frame the opportunities and risks associated with GenAI. The initial findings show a clear shift away from prohibition and surveillance-oriented approaches once common in higher education. Rather than relying on AI detection tools, universities are increasingly emphasising responsible use, transparency, assessment redesign, and shared accountability among students and educators. Academic integrity is being reframed as a matter of learning design and ethical participation rather than solely as compliance and enforcement, moving from a detective to an educative approach. These findings suggest that Australian universities are seeking to balance technological innovation with educational values, offering insights for institutions navigating the evolving relationship between GenAI, assessment, and learning. This paper contributes to ongoing discussions on how higher education can effectively integrate AI while fostering trust, safeguarding academic integrity, and enhancing meaningful learning.

items.title: REVEAL: Reconstructing Video Amodal Content via Language and Flow Guidance
items.abstract: Amodal perception enables humans to perceive entire objects even when parts are occluded, a remarkable cognitive skill that artificial intelligence struggles to replicate. Recent diffusion-based methods have extended amodal completion from images to videos, yet they lack auxiliary priors to guide the reconstruction of heavily occluded content and to maintain temporal consistency over long sequences. We present REVEAL (REconstructing VidEo Amodal content via Language and flow guidance), a unified diffusion-based framework that integrates complementary motion and semantic priors for video amodal completion. A user-provided text query serves a dual role: it drives open-vocabulary video segmentation to obtain visible masks, and it provides semantic guidance for texture reconstruction. For amodal segmentation, we introduce optical flow guidance: by warping visible masks from previous frames to the current frame, the flow-warped mask propagates visible content into occluded regions and approximates the object's current shape, providing a strong shape prior even under simultaneous deformation and occlusion. For texture completion, text guidance constrains the reconstruction of occluded appearance while providing a stable semantic reference that helps maintain visual coherence throughout the reconstruction. We also contribute LAVAT, a new benchmark featuring long video sequences paired with text descriptions, enabling evaluation of text-guided video amodal completion under heavy occlusion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that REVEAL achieves state-of-the-art performance on existing benchmarks while maintaining high-quality temporal consistency over extended sequences. The project page is available at: https://uark-aicv.github.io/REVEAL/.

items.title: Revisiting educational foundations for learning in the age of Generative AI
items.abstract: The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has intensified discussions about assessment assurance, academic integrity, and graduate capability in higher education and vocational education and training (VET). Institutional responses have often prioritised assessment security, while a growing body of scholarship has sought to define the competencies required for AI literacy. This position paper argues that these developments, while important, risk overlooking longstanding educational traditions that remain highly relevant in AI-enabled learning environments. Drawing on critical literacy and Students-as-Partners scholarship, we contend that many capabilities now associated with AI literacy reflect enduring concerns regarding critical evaluation, ethical participation, and learner agency. Rather than proposing another AI-specific framework, we argue that established educational traditions provide a robust foundation for helping students engage with AI critically, ethically, and thoughtfully. We conclude by suggesting that educational responses to AI should prioritise critical dialogue and shared responsibility as students prepare for increasingly AI-enabled professional and social contexts.

items.title: RFW-S: Everyday Deformable Objects with Independent Simulation Verification
items.abstract: Large-scale robotic simulation requires diverse deformable objects with executable physical properties and realistic interaction behaviors. However, existing 3D asset collections primarily emphasize visual diversity, while scalable physical construction and verification remain challenging. We introduce RFW-S, a large-scale dataset of 83,365 simulation-verified assets spanning 485 everyday categories across five structural families: soft solids, cloth sheets, shells, garments, and bags. We develop an automated pipeline integrating reference-guided 3D generation, structure-aware physical modeling, and LLM-assisted parameter estimation and calibration. To ensure physical reliability, we introduce an independent simulation verification framework that evaluates object behaviors under interactions distinct from those used for parameter calibration. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of independent verification and characterize deformable responses under different physical configurations. We further evaluate robotic grasping in terms of both task success and object integrity, and demonstrate the physical realism of our simulated objects through sim-to-real replay of fragile-object manipulation. RFW-S provides a scalable foundation for physically grounded simulation and embodied robotic learning.

items.title: RICoT: Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought for Page Stream Segmentation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have renewed interest in Page Stream Segmentation (PSS), splitting a multi-page file into its constituent documents. Yet published LLM methods still frame the task as boundary classification over one or a few neighboring pages, and commercial document-splitting APIs do not disclose their methods. We reimagine PSS for LLMs as a sequential process over the whole stream and propose RICoT (Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought), a prompting framework that works through the pages as a reader would: within a sliding window it reasons about each page and commits its boundary decision before moving on, and across windows it carries forward a compact record of what it has read, keeping per-call cost bounded. We also introduce FinancePSS-205, a benchmark of 205 real-world, de-identified financial page streams, to be released publicly. On FinancePSS-205, RICoT matches or outperforms pairwise and windowed prompting with the same backbone for each of three open-weight LLMs; on a TABME test subset, RICoT with GLM-5 reaches document F1 0.847 and boundary F1 0.915, above published zero-shot results. A 2B-parameter student, trained on a larger teacher's decisions with and without the page-level reasoning, performs comparably in both modes and comes within 0.05 document F1 of the strongest prompted model on FinancePSS-205.

items.title: Right Diagnosis, Unsafe Route: Auditing Clinical AI Decision Trajectories and Corrective Oversight for Validity and Potential Harm
items.abstract: A clinical AI system can reach a correct final diagnosis through intermediate decisions that could have harmed the patient, and can repair an error while introducing new risks. Most evaluations score final diagnoses; even stepwise benchmarks, which release a case's evidence over time, score whether systems reach the right diagnosis or gather the right information, not whether the decisions a patient passes through are safe. We make patient safety the target of stepwise evaluation. A trajectory audit replays real admissions checkpoint by checkpoint, lets each system decide with only the evidence released so far, and rates every test, treatment and disposition for its potential harm to the patient and, separately, for clinical validity, against the documented final diagnosis and physician-written disease rubrics yet on the evidence available when the decision was made. An LLM judge scores every decision, and a physician reference standard (triple annotation and senior adjudication of a stratified sample) calibrates the rates. An oversight audit branches each trajectory at its first actionable error and measures, on the same branches, whether corrective feedback repairs the error and whether it introduces new harm. Across 300 cases from a hospital cardiology cohort, MIMIC-IV and the public ASCENT benchmark, with up to seven AI systems per source, 55.2% of hospital trajectories reaching an acceptable final diagnosis passed through a decision with moderate or severe potential harm and 24.8% through a clinically unacceptable one; the harm rates were 76.2% on MIMIC-IV and 39.6% on ASCENT. Structured corrections resolved 73.6% of first errors versus 24.8% after bare rejection, yet new potentially unsafe decisions followed 30.2% of corrections versus 19.7% of rejections. A correct final diagnosis does not certify a safe trajectory, and a successful correction does not certify a safe recovery.

items.title: Riscos ocupacionais e saúde mental de professores: uma revisão integrativa da literatura
items.abstract: Teaching work is complex and multifaceted, involving demands that go beyond teaching and may favor occupational risks and mental health problems. This study aims to analyze scientific evidence on occupational risks and their repercussions on teachers’ mental health, characterizing the studies, describing their physical and psychological repercussions, verifying differences according to sex or gender, and analyzing coping, prevention, and intervention strategies. Methodologically, this is an integrative literature review, with a search in the Scopus database, from 2021 to 2026, in Portuguese and Spanish, which yielded 36 articles. Original full-text articles on basic education and/or higher education teachers were included, with data related to occupational risks or health problems. Quantitative, observational, and cross-sectional studies predominated. Thematic analysis organized the findings into risk factors, mental and physical repercussions, sociodemographic differences, and protective strategies. The main risk factors were work overload, role conflict and ambiguity, low autonomy, insufficient social support, technostress, work–family conflict, school violence, and career precariousness. The repercussions included burnout, Common Mental Disorders, anxiety, depression, insomnia, psychological distress, musculoskeletal pain, and vocal fatigue. Gender differences were observed, with greater female vulnerability due to the double workday, and variations according to educational level, with emphasis on academic productivism in higher education and postgraduate studies. Protective strategies combined individual resources, collective integrative practices, and institutional and ergonomic measures, although individual resources are insufficient without structural changes. Thus, teacher illness is multidetermined and articulates organizational demands, interpersonal relationships, and individual resources. Mental health promotion requires permanent institutional policies, reduced overload, social support, ergonomic adequacy, and spaces for listening. Finally, longitudinal studies and searches in multiple databases are recommended.

items.title: Robotic-assisted surgery and artificial intelligence in female infertility: a clinical maturity framework for evidence-based integration
items.abstract: Abstract Background Female infertility often requires coordinated diagnostic, surgical, and assisted reproductive strategies. Robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) may facilitate selected fertility-preserving procedures, while artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to reproductive imaging, embryo assessment, ovarian stimulation, prognosis, and clinical decision support. The clinical evidence for both technologies is uneven, and direct AI integration into robotic infertility surgery remains early. Main body This critical review evaluates current evidence for RAS in myomectomy, tubal reanastomosis, endometriosis surgery, adhesiolysis, ovarian surgery, and selected reconstructive procedures, alongside clinically relevant AI applications in assisted reproduction and reproductive imaging. RAS may offer technical advantages in complex cases through enhanced visualization, instrument articulation, ergonomics, and suturing, but superiority over expert conventional laparoscopy for cumulative live birth, time to pregnancy, ovarian reserve preservation, and cost-effectiveness remains insufficiently established. AI can improve standardization and prediction, but many models remain retrospective, internally validated, incompletely calibrated, or insufficiently tested for clinical utility. We propose a clinical maturity framework that distinguishes current surgeon-controlled RAS from research-stage AI support and speculative autonomous surgery. The most plausible near-term AI-RAS integration is clinician-supervised support for preoperative imaging, surgical difficulty prediction, intraoperative video analytics, robotic skill assessment, postoperative fertility prognosis, and sequencing of surgery and assisted reproductive technology. Conclusion AI and RAS may become complementary components of female infertility care, but routine integrated use requires multicenter prospective validation, standardized infertility-specific outcomes, transparent AI reporting, patient-centered evaluation, regulatory oversight, and assessment of cost and equity.

items.title: Safety II: An Old Perspective on New Problems
items.abstract: The article analyzes the concept of resilient safety (Safety II) proposed by the Danish psychologist Erik Hollnagel, one of the leading specialists in the field of safety and reliability of sociotechnical systems. Despite the authority of this concept, the analysis shows that it has an almost exclusively technical and formalized orientation, which leads it beyond the subject matter of psychology and results in the loss of its psychological content. The approach under consideration focuses on a type of accident resulting from the coincidence of unlikely events, known as functional resonance, and on the FRAM method for identifying the conditions under which it occurs. The article describes the subject context of the problem, namely the technical and engineering-psychological approaches to the safety problem, which makes it possible to assess Hollnagel’s concept as a new attempt to describe the role of the human factor in sociotechnical systems through the projection of technical categories onto it, as was the case in the early 1960s. Thus, the opposition between reactive and proactive approaches is borrowed from risk management. The FRAM “what-if” method is analogous to the methods developed in reliability theory for constructing “success scenarios” and “accident scenarios,” such as HAZOP, HAZID, SIL, and others. The “aspects” of a function, namely input, time, output, resource, control, and precondition that structure risk identification under the FRAM method are functionally similar to the “guide words” used in HAZOP and similar methods. The search for conditions under which functional resonance may occur is semantically equivalent to identifying beyond-design-basis scenarios, as defined in reliability theory. In general, the FRAM method is aimed at detailing and correcting the formal and role-related aspects of work and at ensuring its maximum compliance with instructions. It does not address the issue of the motivational drivers of an employee’s actions, that is, their specifically psychological mechanisms.

items.title: Sample-efficient Personalization of Large Language Model Alignment with Multidimensional User Preference Data
items.abstract: Preference alignment has become a central tool to align large language models (LLMs) with human values and desired behavior, and its online variant can further advance their capabilities beyond what static data alone offer by repeatedly generating and labeling new responses with human feedback. But costly, time-consuming annotations limit its scalability, making sample efficiency essential, and existing methods typically seek to improve it by expanding coverage of the response space or selecting pairs with the highest uncertainty for comparison. Although they are effective, these methods quantify uncertainty from the perspective of the LLM, which may differ from the uncertainty perceived by the user: a pair can appear highly uncertain to the LLM even when past comparisons from the user already imply a clear ordering. In this paper, we propose multidimensional preference-guided online direct preference optimization (MPG-DPO), which leverages low-cost multidimensional evaluations from automated verifiers on the user historical comparisons to construct a personalized preference cone guiding response selection for online preference alignment. Specifically, it first discards responses that are confidently dominated under the estimated user preference, then selects two responses that are competitive under the retained preference cone yet exhibit the strongest unresolved disagreement. Theoretical analysis shows that, with high probability, the fraction of queries spent on cone-dominated responses vanishes as learning progresses. Experiments across multiple LLM families show that MPG-DPO outperforms strong contenders under matched query budgets.

items.title: Scaling Laws for Vision-Language Fusion
items.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as central foundation models combining multimodal perception with text comprehension. While VLMs are traditionally built via late fusion by continued pre-training an off-the-shelf language model on multimodal (image-text) data, mixing modalities from the start of pre-training (early fusion) has recently gained traction. However, the fundamental trade-offs between these paradigms remain poorly understood, resulting in expensive and heuristic-driven training recipes. In this paper, we systematically analyze the learning dynamics of these multimodal pre-training processes, showing that validation losses during vision-language fusion can be modeled by separating the base learning trajectory, where different data types contribute at distinct rates, from a distribution shift driven by the competition between modalities. We derive a scaling law that unifiedly describes these dynamics, enabling accurate loss predictions across mixture ratios, training steps, and model sizes. Crucially, our law characterizes the trade-off between early and late fusion: under a fixed data budget, early fusion preserves text performance while late fusion favors vision performance, yielding a trade-off that increasingly tilts toward early fusion as model size scales. Extensive experiments confirm that our scaling law reliably captures multimodal learning dynamics and governs fusion decisions.

items.title: Scoping review of digital pathology for neoadjuvant rectal cancer response
items.abstract: Aim: Neoadjuvant therapy for locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) yields variable patient responses. Artificial intelligence (AI) and digital pathology offer a novel approach to preoperatively predict treatment outcomes using histomorphological features, potentially guiding organ-preserving strategies. This scoping review maps the current literature on AI-driven neoadjuvant response prediction in LARC to evaluate algorithmic performance and identify methodological gaps. Methods: Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines, a structured search of PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library was conducted for studies published within the last 10 years. Studies applying AI algorithms to pretreatment whole-slide images (WSIs) to predict neoadjuvant response in LARC were included. Results: Eleven publications were included. Ten studies used retrospective cohorts only, whereas one study also included a prospective validation cohort of 100 patients. Algorithmic frameworks predominantly featured classical machine learning, using software extraction of predefined features, and deep learning for autonomous pixel analysis. Across heterogeneous endpoints and cohorts, standalone classical machine-learning models reported external validation area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.811-0.908 (prospective: 0.733), a hybrid microenvironment model reported external AUCs of 0.643-0.656 (prospective: 0.630), and standalone deep-learning models reported an external AUC of 0.723 (internal: 0.710-0.81). Critical limitations across the field include heterogeneous clinical target endpoints, inconsistent baseline staging, and a reliance on “black box” algorithms lacking true biological explainability. Conclusion: AI-driven digital pathology demonstrates strong potential for predicting neoadjuvant treatment response in LARC. However, safe clinical implementation will require standardized endpoints, multimodal integration, and prospective multi-centre validation of algorithms anchored in verifiable tumour biology.

items.title: SEAM: Computer-Use Agents Know the Harm Between Screens, and Commit It Anyway
items.abstract: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) place the harm either in the intent of the task or on a single screen: a malicious instruction, an injected command, a phishing page. An agent that checks the task and each screen in isolation can pass them, so they do not test whether it combines facts seen on different screens. Yet in delegated work, harm often arises exactly this way: a fact about a person on one screen, a fact about an item on another, and a legitimate task that binds them. We introduce SEAM (Safety Execution Across Multiple screens), a benchmark of such cross-screen compositional harm: 600 multi-step, cross-application OSWorld tasks in which the instruction and every single observation are benign and only their combination is harmful. Minimal-pair variants that differ in one place, scored from the server log rather than by an LLM judge, locate where an agent fails. General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs, yet decline when the user states it in one sentence. Agents open the decisive pages, so exposure is not the primary bottleneck. Asked about those pages, they flag the harm, and with thinking they often write the conflict into their reasoning and confirm anyway. Safety recognition thus does not reliably translate into safe execution, and the translation depends on the information channel: the same warning stops agents far more often in the user's instruction than on screen. Proprietary models are markedly more cautious. We release SEAM with its generator and quality gates at https://yuxuan2003.github.io/SEAM/ .

items.title: Sequential Federated Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models for Clinical Outcome Prediction in Intensive Care Units
items.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) show promise for clinical outcome prediction in the intensive care unit (ICU), but collaborative fine-tuning across hospitals is constrained by privacy and data-governance concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative training without exchanging raw data, but conventional parallel FL requires coordinated participation and centralized aggregation, which can be challenging when institutions differ in training availability. We develop and evaluate a novel framework called sequential federated fine-tuning (SFF) framework that enables efficient and privacy-aware collaborative clinical outcome prediction in ICUs across multiple hospitals. By transferring low-rank adapters sequentially from one hospital to the next, SFF supports asynchronous learning, allowing institutions to remain offline until their turn while another institution performs local training. Using 45,149 ICU stays from 27 hospitals in the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD), we applied low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and compared SFF with centralized fine-tuning, local fine-tuning, zero-shot prompting, and federated averaging (FedAvg) for in-hospital mortality and three-class length-of-stay (LoS) prediction. SFF achieved performance close to centralized fine-tuning while outperforming local training and FedAvg. For mortality prediction, SFF reached AUROCs of 86.08% and 89.24% for Qwen-2.5-7B and LLaMA-3.1-8B, respectively; for LoS classification, it reached 75.32% and 76.57%. The advantage over FedAvg was observed across most hospital cohorts and remained evident when local training data were limited. Our work advances the practical, privacy-aware deployment of LLMs in multi-institutional clinical settings for collaborative clinical outcome prediction in ICUs.

items.title: Skills Intelligence and Skills-Based Organizing: A Bibliometric Mapping of Two Disconnected Literatures (2000–2026)
items.abstract: Skills-based organizing replaces jobs and credentials with information on skills, which artificial intelligence now extracts from job postings, résumés and human resource records at scale. Whether this information is valid for the decisions it supports depends on whether research on skills intelligence and research on human resource management inform each other. We mapped 3649 documents published between 2000 and 2026, screened with a large language model audited against a human reviewer, using co-citation, bibliographic coupling and permutation benchmarks. Managerial and computational research form separate communities: only 13% of coupling links connect them, against 46% expected by chance, and the divide is sharpest between studies of the same practice, recruitment and selection. Computational research, 71% of output in 2023–2025, is itself split between recruitment technology and labor-market analytics; it validates skill information mainly against annotated text, about one study in seven relates it to outcomes, and almost none evaluate the decisions it informs. Taxonomies such as ESCO and O*NET do not bridge the communities; work analysis is the main bridge. We propose a skills intelligence value chain from data to outcomes, with five testable propositions, an audit protocol that translates regulatory requirements into validity evidence for each link, a data schema and mixed-methods design that integrate natural language processing with work analysis, and a research agenda for validating AI-produced skill information.

items.title: Smart Fume Detection, Extraction, and Filtration System for CNC Laser Machines
items.abstract: This study developed and evaluated a Smart Fume Detection, Extraction, and Filtration System for CNC Laser Machines at Cebu Technological University–Argao Campus to improve airborne contaminant management during laser cutting and engraving. Anchored in the Cyber-Physical Machine Tool framework, sensor-based monitoring, airflow and filtration principles, Sustainable Manufacturing, and Garvin's Eight Dimensions of Quality, the study employed a developmental research design. The prototype integrated MQ-4 and MQ-135 sensors, microcontroller-based control, automated ventilation, warning mechanisms, digital monitoring, and multistage filtration. Data were collected through 20 controlled operational trials involving plywood and acrylic specimens, technical measurement instruments, observation logs, and questionnaire evaluations from 100 purposively selected respondents. Descriptive statistics and inferential tests assessed technical performance, material-based differences, and contaminant reduction. Results demonstrated 91.7% detection accuracy, 91.2% sensor reliability, a 4.28-second response time, 53.9 CFM extraction airflow, and 77.4% filtration efficiency, meeting all established benchmarks. Mean measured fume concentration decreased significantly from 393.29 ppm to 88.97 ppm, representing a 77.38% reduction (p < 0.0001). Significant differences between plywood and acrylic were observed in detection accuracy, response time, airflow, and fume concentrations, but not in sensor reliability or filtration efficiency. The prototype obtained an overall quality rating of 3.82, interpreted as Reliable. Further sensor calibration, extended testing, and contaminant-specific occupational safety validation are recommended. The study supports Sustainable Development Goals 3, 4, 8, 9, and 12 through occupational health, technical education, safer working conditions, industrial innovation, and responsible production. Its sustainability contribution includes improved fume management, adaptable automation, and institutional operating and maintenance guidance, subject to further validation before broader implementation.

items.title: Social displacement and relational andragogy in generative artificial intelligence-enhanced learning and teaching
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is changing how students learn and how they seek support. This conceptual paper develops social displacement theory to explain how GenAI may replace interpersonal encounters that would otherwise contribute to social learning, belonging, and access to future support. It proposes the ABCs of Human-GenAI Support Decision-Making, in which (A) achievement, (B) burdens, and (C) connections shape whether students rely on independent effort, human support, GenAI, or a combination of these resources. It then advances relational andragogy as an institutional response suited to connected adult learning in a digital society. Relational andragogy intentionally cultivates trust, compassion, mattering, psychological safety, and mutuality while preserving learner agency. Through these relational conditions, institutions can support achievement over time, respond compassionately to external burdens, strengthen students’ anchors of connection, and develop more informed human-GenAI support choices. The framework does not assume that human support is always preferable or that GenAI use is inherently harmful. Instead, we distinguish augmentative uses that expand access or prepare students for human interaction from substitutive patterns that may progressively weaken learning communities. Practical and theoretical implications are offered for educators, student support services, institutional policy, and future empirical testing.

items.title: Software-Process Choice and Competence Maintenance Under GenAI
items.abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in software development raises a knowledge-continuity question: how can organizations retain the human competences needed to evaluate, diagnose, and correct software as production is increasingly delegated? This theory-synthesis article connects research on production and evaluation expertise, practice-dependent competence maintenance, and software-process selection. Two literature-grounded conditional propositions identify residual organizational capabilities (P1) and the conditions supporting their continuity over time (P2). Their combined implications are examined through matched Waterfall and Scrum configurations. Prior studies explain when evaluation depends on production, how expertise may deteriorate, and how methods are selected; they do not by themselves determine when a competence-maintenance deficit is imposed by formal process commitments rather than adjustable work arrangements. The synthesis yields a conditional attribution criterion: a limitation can be assigned to the method only if feasible alternatives within that method cannot meet the same requirements under matched constraints. The constructed comparison establishes this distinction, not observed long-term competence retention. Supplementary File S1 provides a five-step managerial decision guide and two worksheets.

items.title: Sophistication without clarity: Student writing versus unedited GenAI delegation
items.abstract: Writing is central to how students develop and demonstrate communicative competence, yet that development is increasingly difficult to observe as GenAI enters the writing process. This paper establishes a pre-GenAI stylistic baseline of student academic writing and characterises how unedited GenAI responses to the same assessment prompts differ from it. Using stylometric and writing analytics techniques, we analysed over 118,000 words collected in 2021 from 18 higher education students in a software engineering subject. Study 1 used the seven students who completed all four tasks to establish a within-cohort reference: the size and direction of stylistic change in the same students’ writing across two semesters and two rhetorical genres. Study 2 paired each of 59 authentic submissions with a length-matched, zero-shot response to the identical prompt from three large language models. Student writing moved toward shorter words, fewer rare terms and markedly higher readability. Unedited model outputs moved in the opposite direction on each measure, gaining lexical sophistication through a narrower working vocabulary at substantial cost to readability; the human–GenAI gap in readability exceeded the students’ own shift between semesters.

items.title: SpatialCast: Reading the 3D World via Cast Shadows
items.abstract: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) advance toward understanding and interacting with the physical world, spatial reasoning becomes essential for understanding scene structure and anticipating the effects of physical changes. Existing spatial benchmarks have made substantial progress in evaluating spatial relations, memory, and viewpoint reasoning, but less systematically assess how models connect physical scene conditions with visual observations. We introduce SpatialCast, a benchmark that uses cast shadows to evaluate this ability. Cast shadows provide observable evidence of a 3D scene. Their image appearance depends on object geometry and pose, illumination, and viewpoint. We examine this relationship through three complementary tasks that assess scene-projection consistency, predict intervention-induced changes, and infer the physical changes behind visual transitions. The benchmark contains 21,000 synthetic questions with separate scene and geometry test partitions, complemented by 200 SpatialCast-Real questions from 20 photographed scenes. Evaluations show that closed-source MLLMs outperform general-purpose open-weight MLLMs and MLLMs designed for spatial reasoning, which remain near chance on the synthetic benchmark, while even strong closed-source models struggle with shadow-length and light-height judgments. We also use SpatialCast training data for GRPO post-training, improving open-weight MLLM performance on the benchmark. Further evaluations show improvements on several external spatial benchmarks, suggesting transfer of the learned capabilities. These experiments support SpatialCast as a controlled resource for diagnosing spatial reasoning capabilities and studying their learning and generalization.

items.title: StreamChar: Long-Horizon Streaming Character Audio-Video Generation with Decoupled Orchestration
items.abstract: Real-time streaming joint audio-video generation for character animation requires a generator to speak the requested transcript, maintain visual identity across chunks, and run within a strict playback budget. These requirements are difficult to satisfy simultaneously: chunk-wise autoregressive generation can accumulate transcript-audio misalignment and visual drift, while the few-step distillation needed for low latency often degrades spatial diversity and temporal quality. We present StreamChar, a streaming framework that separates long-horizon orchestration from short-window audio-video denoising. An LLM-based orchestrator uses the transcript and historical context to produce frame-aligned audio conditions, and a joint audio-video DiT performs local bidirectional denoising with reference and motion-frame conditioning. For efficient deployment, we use a two-stage distillation pipeline that first compresses the sampler and then fine-tunes the student under online chunk rollouts. A progress-aware pointer aligns partial transcripts with generated audio during rollout training, and a sink-chunk memory provides a persistent visual anchor for reducing long-horizon drift. Experiments on short-clip and long-horizon protocols show that StreamChar runs in real time on a single H100 GPU and provides a favorable system-level trade-off among transcript fidelity, audio-visual synchronization, visual quality, and streaming stability compared with recent joint and audio-driven baselines.

items.title: Student use and perceptions of AI: Findings from a 2026 multi-institutional survey
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is now a common feature of many students’ study practices, and universities are grappling with its implications for assurance of learning, assessment, academic integrity, effective teaching, student support, and policy. Yet institutional responses are still often shaped by assumptions about student use, capability, trust, integrity, and learning (e.g., Bearman & Fawns, 2024). This project is part of the overall Student Perspectives on AI in Higher Education Project, a four-university collaboration investigating how higher education students in Australia understand and use GenAI in relation to themselves as learners. It included two large scale surveys in 2024 (Chung et al., 2024) and 2026. The 2024 phase of the project showed that GenAI had already become embedded in students’ academic practices, with over 80% of surveyed students in four Australian universities having used it for study-related tasks and nearly half using it regularly (Chung et al., 2026). However, the findings also revealed complex patterns of trust, usefulness, self-directed learning, equity, academic integrity, and pragmatic, task-specific engagement. While this 2024 survey provided an initial snapshot of student engagement with GenAI, the rapid pace of technological and institutional change necessitated a follow-up survey in 2026 for an updated understanding of student practices and experiences. The 2026 survey was adapted from the 2024 instrument and comprised 50 questions and 115 items across demographics, use and usefulness, motivations, assessment and academic integrity, learning and fluency, and perceived impact (Henderson et al., 2026). The survey received 10,222 student responses, with 8,700 students fully completing the survey. The sample included 73% undergraduate students, 75% students aged 18 to 24, 59% women, 29% students who spoke a language other than English at home, 19% first-in-family students, and 24% students who identified as having a disability, health condition, or as neurodivergent. This Pecha Kucha presents descriptive findings from the 2026 survey and, where appropriate, compares these with findings from 2024. The recent 2026 data suggest that student use of AI for study has become more frequent: 20% of students reported daily use and 35% weekly use, compared with 13% daily and 31% weekly in 2024. The most common uses include editing or improving writing, generating ideas or examples, teaching students how to do something, finding information or conducting research, and getting feedback on work. Further, the presentation explores new areas of inquiry introduced in 2026, including AI summarisation of course materials, motivations for using or limiting AI, and AI fluency and learning. Among students who used AI for study, the strongest reasons for use were that it made things faster, helped them get unstuck, made things easier, reduced stress, and increased confidence. The strongest reasons for limiting or avoiding AI included concerns about inaccuracy, personal learning values, wanting to do the work themselves, worry about breaking rules, and ethical concerns. By presenting emerging 2026 findings alongside selected 2024 comparisons, this presentation argues that student voices are essential to developing sustainable, ethical, and educationally meaningful institutional responses to AI in higher education.

items.title: TaleBridge: An AI-Mediated System for Supporting Perspective Taking and Creative Subjectivity in Children’s Asynchronous Collaborative Storytelling
items.abstract: Intelligent tools for children’s storytelling support idea generation and multimodal expression, yet most prioritize individual creation over peer collaboration. This study investigates how AI can support children’s asynchronous collaborative story writing while preserving their creative subjectivity. Through a formative study, we derived five design goals and developed TaleBridge, an AI-mediated system combining private ideation spaces, shared negotiation mechanisms, AI-generated textual and visual scaffolds, and a reflection module. In a within-subjects user study, we compared the full version with a baseline version retaining asynchronous writing, co-writing, and plot decomposition. Final stories produced with the full version were shorter and contained fewer plot events, while no statistically significant difference in narrative logic ratings was detected between conditions. Expert ratings indicated higher creative subjectivity, and children reported more positive collaborative experiences. TaleBridge’s overall configuration may support children in examining, comparing, and negotiating each other’s narrative intentions, while leaving creative decisions to children.

items.title: Teacher–GenAI partnership in design and technology education: From utility to allyship
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping Design and Technology (D&T) education by transforming how design ideas are generated, evaluated, and refined. Although existing research has largely focused on capabilities and limitations of AI, less is known about the emerging teacher–GenAI relationships during authentic design practice. Through semi-structured and recall interviews, classroom observations, reflective journals, design folios and artefacts, this qualitative case study investigated these relationships. Guided by sociomaterial perspectives and using reflexive thematic analysis, the study examined how creativity, agency, knowledge construction, pedagogy, and ethical decision-making emerged through human–GenAI interaction. Findings revealed that pre-service teacher–GenAI partnerships evolved through a developmental trajectory from utility, to dialogue, to teacher orchestration, and ultimately allyship. Rather than functioning as a solution-generating tool, GenAI became a provocateur and generative partner whose educational value emerged through iterative cycles of prompting, critique, reflection, and redesign. The study proposes Orchestrated Co-Agency and the Teacher–GenAI Relationship Continuum as complementary conceptual lenses for understanding these interactions. These lenses could offer new theoretical insights into human–AI co-creation and inform curriculum, pedagogy, and the responsible integration of GenAI in Design and Technology education.

items.title: Teaching and assessing reflective writing in generative AI-mediated higher education: Vignettes and provocations
items.abstract: This Pecha Kucha presentation offers a situated account of teaching and assessing in the evolving context of generative AI-mediated higher education. It aims to open up space for contemplation and dialogue around the complexities of the current teaching and learning landscape, where students and educators alike are grappling with new norms, and much grace and understanding needs to be extended on both sides as each learns from, and with, the other how to better navigate the complex nuances and permutations of AI-mediated academic work. Drawing on experiences from a postgraduate academic writing course that I teach, I share a selection of pedagogical vignettes and provocations emerging from my marking of the end-of-semester reflection assignments for the course. This assignment, requiring students to highlight key insights gained from the course and to reflect on these with reference to course discussions and their own scholarly practices, is one that I have greatly enjoyed marking over the years. However, vastly different patterns of engagement have been emerging from the students in recent semesters, and it seems evident that the affordances of generative AI, in changing how students tackle academic assignments, are at the same time disrupting some of higher education’s long-held assumptions about what constitutes learning, writing, and ownership. The pedagogical encounters highlighted include: students asking my own course chatbot to reflect on the course for them, reflections being flagged by AI-detection software as being potentially entirely AI-generated, diverse understandings regarding what constitutes one’s “own work” where AI has been used to assist in the writing process, and students unquestioningly accepting AI’s reformulations as “better” than their own (even when they were not). Encountering these has caused frustration, but I also see in these examples deeper epistemological and pedagogical tensions. Literacy scholars, particularly those working within an “Academic Literacies” perspective (e.g. Jones et al., 1999; Lea & Street, 1998; Lillis, 2003), have long argued that reading and writing are “social practices.” They are, in other words, situated within, influencing and being influenced by, the social and cultural contexts in which they take place. The educational landscape of today, with its myriad AI-assisted possibilities, raises questions of whether, how, and to what extent, our conceptions about “learning,” “writing,” and “ownership” may need recalibration. In fact, scholars have begun to recognise that current writing practices resulting in hybrid texts co-constructed by humans and AI are making it difficult, if not impossible, to identify distinct boundaries between AI-generated output and a student’s own intellectual efforts (e.g. Eaton, 2023; Wu et al., 2026). Higher education is in a season where excitement, curiosity, and unease about generative AI’s impact on academic work and learning sit in tension. Even as one who has actively sought to engage students in discussions of how we can productively and legitimately use generative AI in our writing, I found myself having unexpected reactions (of relief) when I encountered assignments with linguistic infelicities of the sort that suggested their writers had not used generative AI. The way forward, this presentation suggests, requires an intentional commitment to prioritise pedagogical approaches that foreground human connection – both in terms of cultivating a renewed intellectual and emotional connection of students with their own work, and in terms of building connection between students and instructors through open dialogue and compassionate, nuanced approaches to teaching and assessing.

items.title: Teaching beyond AI: Gamified problem-based formative assessment aligned with UNESCO AI competency frameworks
items.abstract: The arrival of capable generative AI (GenAI) tools has posed a genuine and largely unresolved challenge for summative assessment in higher education. When AI-generated submissions evade institutional detection 94% of the time and examination scores rise sharply without any change in teaching, the evidentiary basis of take-home and invigilated assessment is genuinely in question. This paper draws on two lines of work to argue that classroom-based gamified problem-based formative assessment (GPBFA) offers a more durable response than detection-focused approaches. The first line is an empirical study of saval.app, a GPBFA platform evaluated through Keller’s ARCS motivational model across a full university semester (pre n = 41, post n = 44). Results across all four ARCS dimensions were encouraging (all p < .0001; Cronbach’s alpha > .93; composite 81% positive response rate), with near-zero motivational decline across 12 weeks. The second line is a review of UNESCO’s 2024 AI Competency Frameworks for Teachers and Students, which we argue are philosophically and pedagogically aligned with classroom GPBFA in ways the existing literature has not yet made explicit. Taken together, we suggest that moving assessment into the classroom — where it is live, observed, and problem-centred — may address both the integrity challenge and the AI literacy imperative that UNESCO frameworks define.

items.title: TempQuant: Learning Adaptive Temperatures for Quantized Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed at low precision, yet quantization can degrade their performance. We study how quantization interacts with decoding settings such as the sampling temperature and top-p by examining how it distorts the model's next-token probabilities. Measuring entropy during generation across deployed temperatures, we find that quantization warms the model on average, and that temperature matters much more for the performance of a quantized model than for its full-precision counterpart. Because quantization and temperature both shape the next-token distribution, we investigate how much the sampling settings can undo what quantization changes, through our method TempQuant, which learns the quantized model's temperature and top-p to bring its next-token probabilities closer to the full-precision model's. We learn these settings at two granularities. The first is a single global setting per requested temperature, which finds nearly the same temperatures that tuning on labeled answers would, without any labels. Model cards typically recommend sampling a quantized model with the same settings as its full-precision counterpart, while we find that different settings can substantially improve its accuracy. On 3-bit Qwen3-4B, for example, global TempQuant raises MATH accuracy from 34% under the configuration recommended for Qwen's quantized releases to 51%. The second sets the temperature and top-p for every token, motivated by our finding that tokens whose rankings flip under quantization tend to need warming, while tokens whose rankings are preserved tend to need cooling. When quantization degrades accuracy substantially, TempQuant recovers much of it, and when degradation is lighter, it still brings the quantized model's behavior closer to the full-precision model's.

items.title: THE APPLICATION OF GAMIFICATION IN LITERATURE EDUCATION: IMPROVING STUDENTS' MOTIVATION AND ENGAGEMENT
items.abstract: This article examines the application of gamification in literature education as a means of increasing students' motivation and engagement. It analyses the theoretical foundations of gamification, including self-determination theory and game-based learning principles, and describes a quasi-experimental study in which game elements such as points, levels, badges, quests and narrative roles were integrated into literature lessons. The findings indicate that a carefully designed gamified environment strengthens intrinsic motivation, encourages regular reading, improves participation in discussions and deepens students' interpretation of literary texts.

items.title: The apprenticeship layer: What assessment reform cannot secure on its own
items.abstract: Australian higher education has responded to generative artificial intelligence with an ambitious program of assessment reform. Structural approaches, most visibly the two-lane model, seek to sustain trust in degrees by securing some assessments while opening others to AI partnership. This conceptual paper argues that the reform consensus, now sharpened by sector attention to assurance of learning and adaptive capabilities, addresses validity more directly than formation. Assessment tasks are not only measurement occasions; they can also be sites of the cognitive work through which capability develops. Drawing on cognitive apprenticeship, desirable difficulties and cognitive offloading, the paper introduces the apprenticeship layer: the stratum of entry-level cognitive work through which expertise has historically been developed and renewed. As AI is increasingly used to perform parts of this work in workplaces and universities, institutions face a risk of certifying capabilities without reliably preserving the practice through which those capabilities are formed. The paper proposes three principles for formation-centred design: friction by design, process as both learning and evidence, and a care floor of guaranteed human attention. It concludes that valid judgement and capability formation are different questions that assessment can and should be designed to answer together.

items.title: The cost of trust: Human-centred learning design when the process gets fast
items.abstract: Designing an undergraduate systems thinking course in 2023 took months. Workshops, whiteboards, an academic drafting offline, iteration, constructive alignment, compliance, and endless box-moving on a digital canvas. One decision shaped the course: the learning designer judged 10 assessment submission points across 12 weeks excessive and argued to reduce them. The academic, who had taught the discipline for years, refused. Systems thinking concepts interlock, and a student who has not grasped one cannot proceed. The checkpoints were not overload; they were scaffolding. The design bent to the discipline, and the disciplinary expert was right. Generative AI could now compress much of that. It can propose a structure, recommend staggered low-stakes checkpoints for interdependent concepts, and draft the content beneath them. It might well have reached that assessment design faster. Learning designers are tempted to insist something irreplaceable is lost. Much of it is not: a considerable portion of that time was drag, and automating drag is a good outcome. The argument here is not that slowness was valuable. What mattered was less visible. Working on unfamiliar material, the learning designer frequently does not understand the subject. This is usually treated as a limitation. It is better understood as an instrument. The designer is an authentic novice, and their confusion is diagnostic: when an explanation fails for them, it will fail for a student (Wieman, 2007). This is the logic of usability testing: a designer cannot test an interface they already know (Nielsen, 1993). A language model can usefully simulate a novice reader. What it cannot replace is genuine uncertainty: having absorbed the discipline, it fills gaps silently rather than experiencing them. But the instrument only works under a particular social condition. To say “I do not understand this” to an academic, repeatedly, about their own subject, requires standing, which no third space role description confers (Whitchurch, 2008). It is built through months of meetings, shared frustration, and accumulated trust, and it is what made the academic willing to re-explain rather than dismiss. The re-explanation is where the design insight came from. This is the uncomfortable possibility. The inefficiency was not valuable in itself, but the relationship formed inside it, and the relationship is the precondition for the human contribution. Compress the process into an afternoon and the drag disappears, along with the conditions in which trust is made. We have no way to tell which parts of a slow process were waste and which were connection. This Pecha Kucha presents a real course design, concedes what AI could do faster, and identifies what it cannot replace: genuine uncertainty, professional judgement, and trust. For institutions adopting AI-supported workflows, the practical implication is to protect time for co-design and explanation, treating relationship-building as work rather than overhead. It closes with a question beneath the debates about AI and the third space workforce (Bearman et al., 2023; Huijser et al., 2024): if the relationship was produced by the inefficiency we are now eliminating, can human-centred design survive its own optimisation?

items.title: The decommodification paradox: value co-creation and institutional work in a non-monetary peer-to-peer service
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how value is co-created and how trust and coordination are institutionally sustained in a peer-to-peer (P2P) service in which monetary exchange is prohibited at the operational core. Service-dominant (S-D) logic has increasingly theorised value co-creation as coordinated by institutional arrangements within service ecosystems, yet the institutional arrangements it has examined are overwhelmingly market-based. Taking World Wide Opportunities on Organic Farms (WWOOF) as a critical case, the study develops the concept of the decommodification paradox: the co-existence of a non-monetary dyadic exchange with monetary elements at adjacent layers of the service ecosystem, sustained through participants' ongoing institutional work. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative, interpretivist design was adopted. Twenty semi-structured interviews with WWOOF hosts and WWOOFers across 6 Indian states, purposively sampled, were analysed through reflexive thematic analysis. Findings Four themes were generated: (1) value as co-produced labour, learning and dwelling; (2) trust sustained through values-based self-selection, small-community reputation and refusal rather than algorithmic verification; (3) the decommodification paradox, in which the non-monetary dyad is preserved by participants' work of placing monetary elements at the platform and peripheral layers and (4) dark-side dynamics of asymmetry, isolation and gendered labour, read as value co-destruction at the interfaces between layers, that mark the arrangement's boundary conditions. Originality/value The study reframes decommodification in P2P services as a layered property of a service ecosystem rather than a binary attribute of an institution, extends the institutional turn in S-D logic to non-market coordination, identifies the practices that maintain such arrangements and positions the paradox against hybrid-economy, pseudo-sharing and value co-destruction perspectives.

items.title: THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN AN ORDINARY TENNIS PLAYER AND A CHAMPION
items.abstract: This study examines the role of psychology in sports performance, with a particular focus on tennis, an individual sport characterized by intense mental pressure and constant self-regulation. Since psychology became a modern science through the work of Wilhelm Wundt, researchers have explored how thoughts, emotions, and behavior influence human performance. In tennis, psychological factors often determine the difference between an ordinary player and a champion. Based on Pierre Janet’s concept of “conduct,” every action, reaction, and decision made by a tennis player represents an attempt to adapt to competitive situations and manage internal tension. The paper highlights the importance of sensory-perceptive processes in tennis performance. Ordinary players generally display synthetic perception, meaning they are easily distracted by external factors such as crowd noise, weather conditions, or previous mistakes. They often attribute errors to external causes rather than analyzing their own actions. In contrast, champions demonstrate analytical perception, allowing them to focus selectively on relevant details, such as ball speed, body positioning,and the opponent’s movements. Champions also possess advanced mental representation abilities, enabling them to anticipate future actions and strategically plan points before they begin. Another major aspect discussed is stress and emotional regulation. For ordinary players, stress produces emotional instability, muscular tension, and chaotic thinking, all of which negatively affect technicalexecution and decision-making. Champions, however, are capable of transforming negative emotions such as fear or frustration into motivation and determination. Their ability to quickly forget mistakes and refocus on the next point is essential for maintaining performance under stress. Finally, the paper proposes practical psychological strategies for stress management and performanceimprovement, including positive self-talk, motor skill automation, controlled body language, and concentration rituals. items.title: The everyday ecology of children’s emotional experience
items.abstract: Emotional experiences are fundamental inputs to human development, yet we know surprisingly little about their distribution in everyday life. Research typically characterizes children’s emotional environments using global reports or brief observations, obscuring the real-time contexts in which emotions arise. Here, we used artificial intelligence to automatically transcribe and annotate daylong audio recordings from three samples totaling N=159 families with children aged 5 months-8 years old (48.43% female). Our findings reveal the architecture of children’s everyday emotional environments: positive speech was concentrated during play and music, and 25% of speech segments conveyed frustration, concentrated during routine caregiving. Mothers’ mental health did not predict affective speech, but lower child effortful control predicted more frustration in our toddler sample. Frustration peaked in early toddlerhood, suggesting that children’s growing independence at this age may reorganize family emotional environments. Overall, emotional speech appears to emerge from everyday activity, with meaningful shifts across development.

items.title: The impact of soil microorganisms on soil health: Interrelationships, mechanisms of action, and practical applications
items.abstract: Soil health is essential for sustainable agricultural development, and soil microorganisms play an indispensable role in maintaining and improving it. Soil microbial communities influence soil’s physical, chemical, and biological properties through multiple pathways, including promoting nutrient cycling, improving soil structure, decomposing pollutants, and providing biological control against pathogens and pests. This paper comprehensively reviews the complex relationships between soil microorganisms and soil health, focusing on the key mechanisms by which microbial communities contribute to soil health enhancement. It also analyzes the effects of environmental and human factors on microbial community structure and function. In addition, the study discusses the specific applications of soil microorganisms in agriculture, particularly in bioremediation, microbial fertilizers, and biocontrol agent development. This study aims to reveal how soil microorganisms impact soil health, assess their potential applications in agricultural management, and provide scientific support for sustainable agricultural development and soil resource conservation.

items.title: The Learning Design Manifesto: What we value, resist and might build?
items.abstract: Learning design is increasingly central to higher education, yet practitioners continue to grapple with questions of identity, recognition and collective purpose. Building on previous ASCILITE conversations about professional standards for learning design, this working symposium builds upon previous symposia on this theme to move from questions about what learning designers do to what learning design stands for. Participants will be invited to co-author draft principles for a Learning Design Manifesto, articulating the values, commitments and purposes that should guide the field in a period shaped by generative AI, institutional reform, hybrid education and demands for scalability. Through short provocations based on existing research, guided group work and live synthesis, participants will develop, test and prioritise candidate principles.

items.title: The promise of Kaospilot: Human connection for programmatic AI review
items.abstract: Generative AI has pushed universities to review curriculum at pace and scale, raising urgent questions about assessment, academic integrity and graduate capability. At Monash University, the Programmatic Assessment and AI Review (PAAIR) project required faculties to examine assessment and AI integration at program level. This paper asks how educational designers can support teaching teams to make program-level curriculum decisions while AI practice, policy and disciplinary expectations are still unsettled. We use a practice-based reflective case study methodology across the faculties of Science, Arts and Information Technology. Data sources include workshop designs, curriculum artefacts, participant feedback, program mapping outputs and facilitator reflection. Our analysis examines how Kaospilot methods, including vision backcasting, shared canvases and visible artefacts, created structured conditions for teaching teams to work with uncertainty, surface disciplinary values and make program-scale thinking visible. The cases show both the promise and constraint of adapting Kaospilot methods to faculty-wide change. The method helped create the human conditions for programmatic AI review, but its impact depended on artefacts, documentation, leadership, governance pathways and continuing educational design work. The paper argues that AI curriculum review requires structured social conditions to enact policy settings.

items.title: The Shared Word: Evaluating Language Models on Dutch Word Puzzles
items.abstract: Many LLM benchmarks for languages other than English are translated, multiple-choice, or difficult to score automatically. We introduce The Shared Word (TSW-NL), a Dutch benchmark built around four core principles: it is language-specific, open-vocabulary, human-curated, and deterministically scored. Each puzzle gives three clues that describe different senses or uses of the same Dutch word. The clues are individually ambiguous, requiring the solver to combine evidence across multiple clues. We construct the benchmark from Dutch Wikipedia disambiguation pages, followed by automatic filtering and extensive manual curation. The final dataset contains 222 instances, with three independent human answers per test item. The task is clearly challenging: scores in our human study range from 49.5% to 61.0% and the highest-scoring open-weight model we tested reaches only 39.3%. Many others even score below 20%. At the same time, closed-source models show great progress: GPT-4.1 (April 2025) scores 59.2%, whereas GPT-5.6 Sol with max reasoning scores 88.8%. We believe this task provides a useful addition to Dutch model evaluation, plus a clear recipe that can be applied to construct a similar benchmark for other languages.

items.title: The tension between artificial intelligence and knowledge: Power relations in the policies of universities and publishing organisations
items.abstract: Maintaining academic integrity is a serious issue in higher education, affecting the paradigms governing the production and dissemination of human knowledge. Although a significant body of research has explored the ethics of AI tool usage in higher education settings, these studies have neglected to examine the power relations inherent within them. In response to this issue, this study employs Bourdieu’s theories of symbolic violence and actor-network theory to review the AI usage policies of Australian higher education institutions and mainstream academic journal publishers. Specifically, actor-network theory is first applied to identify the governance networks surrounding AI usage within the technological adoption process, thereby establishing that AI tools act as mediating agents that actively facilitate communication between institutions and users. Furthermore, symbolic violence provides a comprehensive explanation of the means by which power-holding institutions legitimise such governance. In summary, the aim of this inquiry is to expose and challenge the “false pretences” of AI ethics regulations that merely adjust, reinforce and gloss over the status quo, thereby channelling the potential of AI towards justice and combating latent human bias. items.title: The Trust Calibration Points Framework (TCa-P) - A Revised Theory for Trust Calibration in Automation and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Calibrated trust is considered an important factor for human-system interaction in decision-making. However, definitions of calibrated trust are heterogeneous and research often lacks conceptual clarity. In our work, we conducted a theoretical integration to summarize approaches defining and operationalizing calibrated trust in automation and AI. We then mapped these approaches onto the trust development process that builds on the Trustworthiness Assessment Model (Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025) and the Organizational Trust Model (Mayer et al., 1995). The resulting Trust Calibration Points Framework (TCa-P) offers theoretical clarity and actionable insights for improving trust calibration by identifying six calibration points that can be calibrated to optimize joint human-system performance, and, as a consequence, effective human oversight: maximum joint performance benchmarking, trustworthiness assessment, alignment of individual standards, risk-benefit assessment, dispositions, and behavioral adaptation. The TCa-P emphasizes that trust calibration is not monolithic but instead happens at different points along the trust development process.

items.title: The Xaant Resting Autonomic Signature (X-RAS): prospective clinical validation of an autonomic biomarker for anxiety and depressive disorders
items.abstract: Abstract Background Anxiety and depressive disorders affect over 500 million people globally, with a treatment gap exceeding 75% in low- and middle-income countries. Current diagnostic frameworks rely on clinical interview and self-report, with test–retest reliability of 0.20 to 0.67 for these disorders in DSM-5 field trials. Autonomic nervous system dysregulation is a well-established biological correlate of anxiety and depression. We report the first, to our knowledge, prospective clinical validation of an autonomic biomarker-based artificial intelligence system against a blinded psychiatrist reference standard in routine clinical practice. Methods We conducted a prospective, two-site diagnostic accuracy study at tertiary hospitals in Delhi and Kerala, India (CTRI/2023/07/054984). The Xaant Resting Autonomic Signature (X-RAS) platform, a three-layer LSTM with self-attention previously developed on an independent cohort of 2,349 participants and frozen prior to the trial, analysed electrodermal activity and blood volume pulse from 15-minute resting-state recordings and produced a four-class diagnostic classification. Of 180 participants enrolled, 170 completed the protocol. Out of these, 114 clinical participants with DSM-5 depression, anxiety, or comorbid disorders, and 56 reference group participants recruited from a long-term meditation practice tradition were considered. The reference standard was the DSM-5 diagnosis established by the site psychiatrist, who was blinded to the platform output. The primary outcome was Cohen's kappa for AI-psychiatrist diagnostic agreement within the clinical cohort. Results Within the clinical cohort, the platform achieved 93.0% agreement with clinical diagnosis (κ = 0.884, 95% CI 0.789 to 0.956), with 100% sensitivity for generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) detection in the GAD subgroup (n = 15, 95% CI 78.2 to 100). All eight classification disagreements fell along the depression–comorbid boundary, and the AI classification agreed with the patient's own self-categorisation in five of the eight. Performance was consistent across the two sites (Delhi 94.6%, Kerala 91.4%, p = 0.527) and across age, sex, and education subgroups. Classical autonomic markers separated the clinical and reference groups with moderate to large effect sizes (d = 0.53 to 0.84). Two of the physiological constructs of the development-cohort, namely Hypoactivity and Experience, were reproduced at the group level in independently diagnosed patients. A per-minute slope analysis of the tonic EDA signal showed a transdiagnostic reversal, where the baseline settled downward during rest in the reference group and drifted upward across all three clinical subgroups (Kruskal–Wallis p = 3.0 × 10⁻²²). Conclusions Resting-state autonomic AI analysis provides objective diagnostic support for anxiety and depressive disorders, with Cohen’s κ = 0.884 (95% CI 0.789 to 0.956) against psychiatrist-assigned DSM-5 diagnoses in routine outpatient practice. Direct comparison with published inter-rater or test-retest reliability estimates is not appropriate given differences in methodology and reference standards. The platform's low cost, portability, and suitability for non-specialist operators support scalability in resource-limited settings. External validation in primary care, community, telehealth, and non-Indian populations is the next step for the programme. Trial registration: Clinical Trials Registry of India, CTRI/2023/07/054984, registered July 2023.

items.title: Think Before You Code: A Benchmark for Testing LLMs on Software Engineering Deliberation
items.abstract: Think Before You Code (TBYC) is a benchmark pipeline for studying whether code-focused language models can reason about software issues in ways that resemble human engineering deliberation. The benchmark curates GitHub issue discussions into structured records, extracts human discussion artifacts such as problems, solutions, constraints, rationales, and trade-offs, and then prompts models to generate issue-level "thoughts" using retrieved code context and few-shot examples. It converts model responses back into the same artifact space and evaluates them against human annotations using complementary metrics for artifact type detection, metadata matching, tag overlap, and semantic summary similarity. Beyond scoring, this study includes visualization, leaderboard, and baseline tools that make it possible to compare models, prompting strategies, and extraction methods across repositories and issues. Think Before You Code is an end-to-end evaluation environment for measuring how closely LLM software reasoning aligns with human strategic judgment.

items.title: This Looks Like What? Challenges and Future Research Directions for Part-Prototype Models
items.abstract: The growing interest in eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has stimulated research on models with built-in interpretability, among which part-prototype models are particularly prominent. Part-Prototype Models (PPMs) classify inputs by comparing them to learned prototypes and provide human-understandable explanations of the form “this looks like that.” Despite this intrinsic interpretability, PPMs have not yet emerged as a competitive alternative to post-hoc explanation methods. This survey reviews work published between 2019 and 2025 and derives a taxonomy of the challenges faced by current PPMs. The analysis reveals a diverse set of open problems. The main issue concerns the quality and number of learned prototypes. Further challenges include limited generalization across tasks and contexts, as well as methodological shortcomings such as non-standardized evaluation. Five broad research directions are identified: improving predictive performance, developing theoretically grounded architectures, establishing frameworks for human-AI collaboration, aligning models with human concepts, and defining robust metrics and benchmarks for evaluation. The survey aims to stimulate further research and promote intrinsically interpretable models for practical applications. A curated list of the surveyed papers is available at https://github.com/aix-group/ppm-survey .
